subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
Let  

\[
d=n+2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n=d-2 .
\]

The divisibility condition becomes  

\[
d\mid 3\,(n+3)\,(n^{2}+9)=3\,(d+1)\big[(d-2)^{2}+9\big].
\]

Compute  

\[
(d-2)^{2}+9 = d^{2}-4d+4+9 = d^{2}-4d+13 .
\]

Hence  

\[
d\mid 3\,(d+1)(d^{2}-4d+13).
\]

Reduce the right‑hand side modulo \(d\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
3\,(d+1)(d^{2}-4d+13) &\equiv 3\cdot 1\cdot 13 \pmod d\\
&= 39 \pmod d .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
d\mid 39 .
\]

Since \(d=n+2\) and \(n\ge 1\), we have \(d\ge 3\).  
The positive divisors of \(39\) are \(1,3,13,39\); discarding \(1\) we obtain  

\[
d\in\{3,13,39\}.
\]

Corresponding \(n=d-2\) values are  

\[
n = 1,\;11,\;37 .
\]

All satisfy the original divisibility (checked directly).  

The sum of all such positive integers \(n\) is  

\[
1+11+37 = 49 .
\]

\[
\boxed{49}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
The first equation  

\[
|25+20i-z|=5
\]

represents the circle  

\[
(x-25)^2+(y-20)^2=5^2 .
\]

The second equation  

\[
|z-(4+k)|=|z-(3i+k)|
\]

means that \(z\) is equidistant from the points  

\[
P=(4+k,0),\qquad Q=(k,3).
\]

Hence \(z\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{PQ}\).

---

### Equation of the perpendicular bisector  

Midpoint of \(PQ\):

\[
M=\Bigl(\frac{(4+k)+k}{2},\frac{0+3}{2}\Bigr)=\bigl(k+2,\tfrac32\bigr).
\]

Slope of \(PQ\) is \(\displaystyle \frac{3}{-4}=-\frac34\); thus the slope of the perpendicular bisector is \(\displaystyle \frac43\).

Using point–slope form,

\[
y-\frac32 = \frac43\bigl(x-(k+2)\bigr).
\]

Putting this in standard form:

\[
8x-6y-8k-7=0. \tag{L}
\]

---

### Tangency condition  

The line \((L)\) must intersect the circle in **exactly one** point, i.e. be tangent to it.  
The distance from the circle’s centre \(C=(25,20)\) to the line \((L)\) must equal the radius \(5\).

\[
\text{dist}(C,(L))=\frac{|8\cdot25-6\cdot20-8k-7|}{\sqrt{8^{2}+(-6)^{2}}}
   =\frac{|73-8k|}{10}.
\]

Set this equal to \(5\):

\[
\frac{|73-8k|}{10}=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |73-8k|=50.
\]

Thus  

\[
\begin{cases}
73-8k = 50 &\Longrightarrow k=\dfrac{23}{8},\\[4pt]
73-8k = -50 &\Longrightarrow k=\dfrac{123}{8}.
\end{cases}
\]

Both values make the line tangent to the circle, giving exactly one solution for \(z\).

---

### Sum of all possible \(k\)

\[
k_1+k_2=\frac{23}{8}+\frac{123}{8}=\frac{146}{8}= \frac{73}{4}.
\]

Write \(\dfrac{73}{4}\) as \(\dfrac{m}{n}\) with \(\gcd(m,n)=1\); here \(m=73,\; n=4\).

\[
m+n = 73+4 = 77.
\]

\[
\boxed{77}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
Label the vertices of the regular \(24\)-gon by the elements of \(\mathbb Z_{24}\).
If a segment joins vertex \(i\) to vertex \(j\) then the (shorter) circular distance
\(\min\{|i-j|,24-|i-j|\}\) is the same for all 12 segments.
Let that distance be \(m\;(1\le m\le 12)\).

---

### 1.  The graph of possible edges

For a fixed \(m\) consider the graph \(G_m\) whose vertices are \(\mathbb Z_{24}\) and whose
edges are the unordered pairs \(\{i,i+m\}\) (the same as \(\{i,i-m\}\)).
If \(m\neq 12\) each vertex is incident with the two edges
\(i\!\to\! i+m\) and \(i\!\to\! i-m\); the graph consists of
\(\gcd(24,m)\) disjoint cycles, each of length \(\dfrac{24}{\gcd(24,m)}\).

When \(m=12\) each vertex is adjacent to only its opposite vertex, so \(G_{12}\) is already a perfect matching (12 disjoint edges).

---

### 2.  Perfect matchings of \(G_m\)

A set of 12 disjoint segments of length \(m\) corresponds to a **perfect matching**
of \(G_m\).

* If a component of \(G_m\) has odd length, no perfect matching exists.
  This happens exactly when \(\dfrac{24}{\gcd(24,m)}\) is odd, i.e. when
  \(\gcd(24,m)=8\) (the case \(m=8\)).  
  Hence for \(m=8\) there are \(0\) ways.

* Otherwise each component is an even cycle.  
  An even cycle of length \(L\) has exactly two perfect matchings
  (choose alternating edges).  
  With \(\gcd(24,m)\) components, the total number of matchings is  

  \[
  2^{\gcd(24,m)} .
  \]

* For \(m=12\) the graph already consists of 12 isolated edges, giving exactly one matching.

---

### 3.  Counting for each possible \(m\)

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
m & \gcd(24,m) & \text{matchings} \\ \hline
1 & 1 & 2\\
2 & 2 & 4\\
3 & 3 & 8\\
4 & 4 & 16\\
5 & 1 & 2\\
6 & 6 & 64\\
7 & 1 & 2\\
8 & 8 & 0\\
9 & 3 & 8\\
10& 2 & 4\\
11& 1 & 2\\
12& - & 1
\end{array}
\]

---

### 4.  Total number of ways

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Total} &=2+4+8+16+2+64+2+0+8+4+2+1\\
&=113.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus there are  

\[
\boxed{113}
\]

different ways to draw the 12 equal‑length segments so that every vertex of the regular 24‑gon is an endpoint of exactly one segment.

subject: aime_2026
sample_text:
Let  

\[
y=\log_{2026}x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=2026^{\,y}\;(x>0)
\]

The equation  

\[
\sqrt[20]{x^{\log_{2026}x}}=26x
\]

becomes  

\[
\bigl( (2026^{y})^{y} \bigr)^{1/20}=26\cdot2026^{y}
\]

\[
2026^{y^{2}/20}=26\cdot2026^{y}
\]

Divide by \(2026^{y}\):

\[
2026^{\,y^{2}/20-y}=26
\]

Take \(\log_{2026}\) of both sides:

\[
\frac{y^{2}}{20}-y=\log_{2026}26\;=:c .
\]

Hence  

\[
y^{2}-20y-20c=0 .
\]

Solving the quadratic:

\[
y=10\pm\sqrt{100+20c},
\qquad c=\log_{2026}26 .
\]

Both roots give admissible positive \(x\) (since \(2026>1\)).  
The two possible values of \(x\) are  

\[
x_{1}=2026^{\,10+\sqrt{100+20c}},\qquad 
x_{2}=2026^{\,10-\sqrt{100+20c}} .
\]

Their product is  

\[
x_{1}x_{2}=2026^{\,(10+\sqrt{...})+(10-\sqrt{...})}=2026^{20}.
\]

---

### Divisor count of the product  

Factor \(2026\):

\[
2026 = 2\cdot 1013,
\]

where \(1013\) is prime. Hence  

\[
2026^{20}=2^{20}\cdot 1013^{20}.
\]

If \(n = p_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\), the number of positive divisors of \(n\) is  

\[
(a_{1}+1)(a_{2}+1).
\]

Thus  

\[
\tau(2026^{20})=(20+1)(20+1)=21\cdot 21=441.
\]

\[
\boxed{441}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
The six two‑letter words are obtained by first pairing the twelve letters, then writing each pair in alphabetical order and finally listing the six words alphabetically.  
Let the six unordered pairs be \(\{x_i ,y_i\}\;(i=1,\dots ,6)\) with \(x_i<y_i\).  
The alphabetical list of the words is determined by the set of first letters \(\{x_1,\dots ,x_6\}\); the last word is the one whose first letter is the largest among these six “smaller” letters.

Hence the last word contains \(G\) **iff**

* \(G\) is the smaller letter of its pair (so \(G\) appears as the first letter), and  
* no letter larger than \(G\) (\(H,I,J,K,L\)) is a smaller letter of its pair.

Thus every letter among \(\{H,I,J,K,L\}\) must be paired with a letter that is smaller than it (necessarily from \(\{A,B,C,D,E,F,G\}\)), and \(G\) must be paired with a larger letter.

---

### Counting the favourable pairings  

1. **Partner of \(G\).**  
   \(G\) can be paired with any of the five letters \(H,I,J,K,L\). → \(5\) choices.

2. **Pair the remaining four letters \(>G\).**  
   After the partner of \(G\) is chosen, four letters among \(\{H,I,J,K,L\}\) remain.  
   They must each be paired with a distinct letter from \(\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\).  
   *Choose which four of the six smaller letters will be used:* \(\binom{6}{4}=15\) ways.  
   *Match them with the four large letters:* \(4! = 24\) ways.

3. **The two unused small letters pair together.**  
   Once the four small letters are matched, the two left from \(\{A,\dots ,F\}\) must pair with each other – exactly \(1\) way.

Hence the number of favourable pairings is  

\[
5 \times \binom{6}{4} \times 4! = 5 \times 15 \times 24 = 1800 .
\]

---

### Counting all possible pairings  

The total number of ways to partition twelve distinct letters into six unordered pairs is  

\[
\frac{12!}{2^{6}\,6!}= (12-1)!! = 11\cdot9\cdot7\cdot5\cdot3\cdot1 = 10395 .
\]

---

### Probability  

\[
P = \frac{1800}{10395}= \frac{40}{231}\qquad (\text{in lowest terms}).
\]

Thus \(m=40,\;n=231\) and  

\[
m+n = 40+231 = 271 .
\]

\[
\boxed{271}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
From the data we have  

\[
\cos\angle A_iA_1A_{i+1}= \frac{12}{13},
\qquad 
\sin\angle A_iA_1A_{i+1}= \frac{5}{13}.
\]

The area of \(\triangle A_iA_1A_{i+1}\) is  

\[
1=\frac12\;A_iA_1\cdot A_{i+1}A_1\sin\theta
      \Longrightarrow 
      A_iA_1\cdot A_{i+1}A_1=\frac{2}{\sin\theta}
      =\frac{2}{5/13}= \frac{26}{5}\; .
\]

Denote \(r_i=A_iA_1\;(i=2,\dots ,11)\) and set  

\[
C=\frac{26}{5}.
\]

Then for \(2\le i\le10\)

\[
r_i r_{i+1}=C. \tag{1}
\]

Hence the sequence \((r_i)\) is periodic of period \(2\); write  

\[
r_{2}=a,\qquad r_{3}=\frac{C}{a},\qquad r_{4}=a,\; \dots ,\; r_{11}=\frac{C}{a}.
\]

Thus  

\[
A_1A_2+A_1A_{11}=a+\frac{C}{a}=x\qquad\text{(to be found)}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Length of the other sides  

For each \(i=2,\dots ,10\) the side \(d_i=A_iA_{i+1}\) satisfies, by the law of cosines,

\[
d_i^{\,2}=r_i^{\,2}+r_{i+1}^{\,2}-2r_ir_{i+1}\cos\theta .
\]

Using \(\cos\theta=12/13\) and (1),

\[
2r_ir_{i+1}\cos\theta = 2C\cdot\frac{12}{13}= \frac{48}{5},
\]
\[
d_i^{\,2}=r_i^{\,2}+r_{i+1}^{\,2}-\frac{48}{5}.
\]

Because \((r_i,r_{i+1})\) is either \((a,C/a)\) or \((C/a,a)\), all nine lengths
\(d_2,\dots ,d_{10}\) are equal; denote them by \(d\).  Then

\[
d^{2}=a^{2}+\frac{C^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{48}{5}. \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Express everything through \(x=a+\dfrac{C}{a}\)

Notice

\[
a^{2}+\frac{C^{2}}{a^{2}}
   =\Bigl(a+\frac{C}{a}\Bigr)^{2}-2C
   =x^{2}-2C .
\]

Hence from (2)

\[
d^{2}=x^{2}-2C-\frac{48}{5}.
\]

Since \(C=\dfrac{26}{5}\),

\[
2C+\frac{48}{5}= \frac{52}{5}+\frac{48}{5}=20,
\]
so

\[
d=\sqrt{x^{2}-20}. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Use the perimeter  

The perimeter of the 11‑gon is

\[
A_1A_2+A_1A_{11}+9d = x+9d =20 .
\]

Substituting \(d\) from (3):

\[
x+9\sqrt{x^{2}-20}=20.
\]

Let \(t=\sqrt{x^{2}-20}\;(t\ge0)\). Then \(x=20-9t\) and

\[
(20-9t)^{2}=t^{2}+20\Longrightarrow 8t^{2}-36t+38=0
\Longrightarrow 4t^{2}-18t+19=0.
\]

Thus  

\[
t=\frac{18\pm\sqrt{324-304}}{8}
   =\frac{18\pm2\sqrt5}{8}
   =\frac{9\pm\sqrt5}{4}.
\]

If the ‘\(+\)’ sign is taken, \(x\) becomes negative, which is impossible.
Hence  

\[
t=\frac{9-\sqrt5}{4},\qquad 
x=20-9t=\frac{9\sqrt5-1}{4}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Result  

\[
A_1A_2+A_1A_{11}= \frac{9\sqrt5-1}{4}
     =\frac{m\sqrt n-p}{q},
\]
with \(m=9,\;n=5,\;p=1,\;q=4\).

Therefore  

\[
m+n+p+q = 9+5+1+4 = \boxed{19}.
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
Let  

\[
\begin{array}{c}
a=h_2,\; b=h_3,\; c=v_2,\; d=v_3\qquad (\text{interior edges})
\end{array}
\]

where each variable is \(1\) if the edge is red and \(0\) if it is blue.

For the four unit squares \(A,B,C,D\) the required numbers of red edges are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A:&\;h_0+v_0+a+c =2,\\
B:&\;h_1+v_4+b+c =2,\\
C:&\;h_4+v_1+a+d =2,\\
D:&\;h_5+v_5+b+d =2 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus for each square the sum of its two **boundary** edges must equal  

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_A &=2-(a+c),\\
S_B &=2-(b+c),\\
S_C &=2-(a+d),\\
S_D &=2-(b+d).
\end{aligned}
\]

If a required sum is \(0\) or \(2\) the two boundary edges are forced
(only one way); if it is \(1\) the two edges can be \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\) (two ways).
Hence, for a given interior configuration \((a,b,c,d)\),

\[
\text{# colourings} = 2^{N_1},
\]

where \(N_1\) is the number of the four quantities \(S_A,S_B,S_C,S_D\) that equal
\(1\).

Now  

\[
S_A=1\iff a+c=1,\qquad
S_B=1\iff b+c=1,\qquad
S_C=1\iff a+d=1,\qquad
S_D=1\iff b+d=1 .
\]

Thus \(N_1\) counts how many of the four sums  

\[
a+c,\; b+c,\; a+d,\; b+d
\]

are equal to \(1\).

Enumerating the \(2^4=16\) possibilities for \((a,b,c,d)\):

| \(a,b\) | \(c,d\) | \(N_1\) | contribution \(2^{N_1}\) |
|---------|---------|--------|--------------------------|
| \(0,0\) | \(0,0\) | 0 | 1 |
|         | \(1,0\) | 2 | 4 |
|         | \(0,1\) | 2 | 4 |
|         | \(1,1\) | 4 | 16 |
| \(1,1\) | \(0,0\) | 4 | 16 |
|         | \(1,0\) | 2 | 4 |
|         | \(0,1\) | 2 | 4 |
|         | \(1,1\) | 0 | 1 |
| \(0,1\) | any     | 2 | 4 (each of 4 choices) |
| \(1,0\) | any     | 2 | 4 (each of 4 choices) |

Adding all contributions:

\[
25 + 25 + 16 + 16 = 82.
\]

Hence there are  

\[
\boxed{82}
\]

different ways to colour the 12 unit edges so that each of the four unit squares has exactly two red and two blue sides.

subject: aime_2026
sample_text:
The sum can be rewritten as  

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{10^{k}-1}
    =\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{10^{-k}}{1-10^{-k}}
    =\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}10^{-kn}
    =\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}d(m)10^{-m},
\]

where \(d(m)\) is the number of positive divisors of \(m\).

Hence  

\[
10^{100}S=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} d(m)10^{\,100-m}
       =\sum_{m=1}^{100} d(m)10^{\,100-m}
        +\underbrace{\sum_{m=101}^{\infty} d(m)10^{\,100-m}}_{\displaystyle <10 } .
\]

The second sum is less than \(10\), so it contributes no integer part after the
carries are performed; its fractional part never reaches \(1\).

Thus the integer part of \(10^{100}S\) is obtained from the first sum.
Write  

\[
a_i = d(100-i)\qquad (i=0,1,\dots ,99),
\]

so that \(a_0\) is the units digit, \(a_1\) the tens digit, etc.
The values \(a_i\) are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&a_0=9,\ a_1=6,\ a_2=6,\ a_3=2,\ a_4=12,\ a_5=4,\ a_6=4,\ a_7=4,\ a_8=6,\ a_9=4,\\
&a_{10}=12,\ a_{11}=2,\ a_{12}=8,\ a_{13}=4,\ a_{14}=4,\ a_{15}=4,\ a_{16}=12,\ldots
\end{aligned}
\]

(Carried out for all \(i=0\) to \(99\); the list continues as obtained from the
divisor function.)

Now perform the usual base‑10 carries from the least significant digit upward:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
i & a_i+\text{carry in} & \text{digit }(= \bmod 10) \\ \hline
0 & 9  & 9,\ \text{carry}=0\\
1 & 6  & 6,\ \text{carry}=0\\
2 & 6  & 6,\ \text{carry}=0\\
\text{(higher }i) & \dots & \dots
\end{array}
\]

The first three positions already give no carry, and any carry generated at
higher positions can only affect more significant digits, never the units,
tens, or hundreds places.

Hence the last three digits (hundreds, tens, units) of \(\lfloor 10^{100}S\rfloor\)
are \(6,6,9\), i.e. the integer ends with \(669\).

Therefore the remainder when \(\displaystyle\bigl\lfloor10^{100}S\bigr\rfloor\) is
divided by \(1000\) is  

\[
\boxed{669}.
\]

sample_text:
For an arithmetic sequence with first term \(a_{1}=4\) and integer common difference \(d\),

\[
a_{n}=4+(n-1)d .
\]

Since the terms \(24\) and \(34\) must appear, there exist positive integers \(k,l\) such that  

\[
4+(k-1)d=24\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4+(l-1)d=34 .
\]

Thus  

\[
(k-1)d =20,\qquad (l-1)d =30 .
\]

Hence \(d\) divides both \(20\) and \(30\); \(d\) must be a positive divisor of \(\gcd(20,30)=10\).

\[
d\in\{1,2,5,10\}.
\]

For each admissible \(d\) the 10th term is  

\[
a_{10}=4+9d .
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
d=1 &: a_{10}=4+9=13,\\
d=2 &: a_{10}=4+18=22,\\
d=5 &: a_{10}=4+45=49,\\
d=10&: a_{10}=4+90=94.
\end{aligned}
\]

Summing these 10th terms:

\[
13+22+49+94 = 178 .
\]

\[
\boxed{178}
\]

sample_text:
Let  

\[
AB=c=200,\qquad AC=b=225,\qquad BC=a\;(=?).
\]

Denote the point where the internal bisector of \(\angle A\) meets \(BC\) by \(D\).
By the Angle–Bisector Theorem  

\[
\frac{BD}{CD}= \frac{AB}{AC}= \frac{c}{b}= \frac{200}{225}= \frac{8}{9},
\]

so  

\[
BD=\frac{8}{17}a,\qquad CD=\frac{9}{17}a .
\]

Both \(BD\) and \(CD\) must be integers, hence \(a\) is a multiple of \(17\):
\[
a=17k,\qquad BD=8k,\qquad CD=9k,
\]
with \(k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).

---

### Power of a point

The circle \(\omega\) passes through \(A\) and is tangent to \(BC\) at \(D\).
Thus for the external points \(B\) and \(C\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Pow}_B(\omega)&=(BD)^2 = BA\cdot BE,\\[2mm]
\text{Pow}_C(\omega)&=(CD)^2 = CA\cdot CF .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(BA=200\) and \(CA=225\),

\[
BE = \frac{(BD)^2}{200}= \frac{(8k)^2}{200}= \frac{8}{25}k^{2},
\qquad
CF = \frac{(CD)^2}{225}= \frac{(9k)^2}{225}= \frac{9}{25}k^{2}.
\]

Now  

\[
AE = AB-BE = 200-\frac{8}{25}k^{2},
\qquad
AF = AC-CF = 225-\frac{9}{25}k^{2}.
\]

The problem states that \(AE,AF,BD,CD\) are **positive integers**.  
Since \(BD=8k\) and \(CD=9k\) are already integers, we only need
\(AE\) and \(AF\) to be integers.

Write  

\[
AE = \frac{5000-8k^{2}}{25}= \frac{8}{25}\bigl(625-k^{2}\bigr),\qquad
AF = \frac{5625-9k^{2}}{25}= \frac{9}{25}\bigl(625-k^{2}\bigr).
\]

Thus \(625-k^{2}\) must be divisible by \(25\).  
Let  

\[
625-k^{2}=25m\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}),
\]

so

\[
AE = 8m,\qquad AF = 9m .
\]

Then  

\[
k^{2}=625-25m = 25(25-m),
\]
hence \(k\) is a multiple of \(5\).  Write \(k=5n\;(n\ge 1)\).  
From the previous line,

\[
25n^{2}=25(25-m)\Longrightarrow n^{2}=25-m\Longrightarrow m=25-n^{2}.
\]

Because \(m>0\), we need \(n^{2}<25\); thus \(n=1,2,3,4\).

---

### Corresponding values

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
n & k=5n & a=17k & AE=8m & AF=9m\\ \hline
1 & 5   & 85  & 192 & 216\\
2 &10   &170  & 168 & 189\\
3 &15   &255  & 128 & 144\\
4 &20   &340  &  72 &  81
\end{array}
\]

All four cases satisfy the required positivity and integrality
conditions.

Hence the possible lengths of \(BC\) are  

\[
85,\;170,\;255,\;340 .
\]

The problem asks for the sum of all possible values of \(BC\):

\[
85+170+255+340 = 850 .
\]

\[
\boxed{850}
\]

subject: aime_2026
sample_text:
The rectangle is a \(2n\times 2n\) grid with \(n=5\); thus we have a \(10\times 10\) board.  
A cell‑loop is the border of an \(a\times b\) rectangle (\(2\le a,b\le10\)) and uses  

\[
p(a,b)=2a+2b-4=2\,(a+b-2)
\]

cells.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Modelling a tiling by loops  

When a loop is removed, the remaining uncovered region is again a rectangle.
Consequently each loop in a tiling is one of three types  

* **Horizontal strip** – a \(2\times w\) loop (the whole top or bottom rows).  
  It reduces the height by \(2\).  
* **Vertical strip** – a \(h\times 2\) loop (the whole left or right columns).  
  It reduces the width by \(2\).  
* **Perimeter loop** – the whole border of the current rectangle \(h\times w\).  
  It reduces both height and width by \(2\).

Let  

\[
\begin{aligned}
t,b & =\text{number of horizontal strips taken from the top and bottom},\\
\ell ,r & =\text{number of vertical strips taken from the left and right},\\
k & =\text{number of perimeter loops}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All numbers are non‑negative integers and the total number of loops must be five:

\[
t+b+\ell+r+k=5. \tag{1}
\]

After all loops are removed the remaining rectangle has dimensions  

\[
H = 10-2(t+b+k),\qquad  
W = 10-2(\ell+r+k).
\]

The board is completely covered when at least one of these dimensions is zero
(the area is then \(0\)). Hence we need  

\[
H=0\quad\text{or}\quad W=0. \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Solutions with \(H=0\)  

\(H=0\) gives \(t+b+k=5\).  
Using (1) we obtain \(\ell+r=k\) and therefore \(\ell=r=0\).
Thus there are only horizontal strips besides the \(k\) perimeter loops.
The number of horizontal strips is \(5-k\).

The \(k\) perimeters create \(k+1\) “horizontal regions’’ (outside the outermost
perimeter, between successive perimeters, and inside the innermost perimeter).
The \(5-k\) strips can be placed in any of these regions and each strip may be
on the top side or the bottom side of the region.

Hence we must distribute \(5-k\) indistinguishable objects into \(2(k+1)\)
distinguishable boxes, which can be done in  

\[
\binom{(5-k)+2(k+1)-1}{2(k+1)-1}
  =\binom{k+6}{2k+1}
\]

ways.

Summing over \(k=0,1,\dots ,5\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
k=0 &: \binom{6}{1}=6\\
k=1 &: \binom{7}{3}=35\\
k=2 &: \binom{8}{5}=56\\
k=3 &: \binom{9}{7}=36\\
k=4 &: \binom{10}{9}=10\\
k=5 &: \binom{11}{11}=1
\end{aligned}
\]

Total for the case \(H=0\):

\[
6+35+56+36+10+1 = 144 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Solutions with \(W=0\)

By symmetry the same count is obtained when the width becomes zero; the
configuration now consists of vertical strips and \(k\) perimeter loops.
Thus we also obtain \(144\) tilings.

The configuration where both \(H=0\) and \(W=0\) occurs only when
\(k=5\) (five nested perimeters); it has been counted in both totals, so we
subtract it once.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Total number of partitions

\[
\boxed{144+144-1 = 287}
\]

For a function \(\pi:A\to A\) with \(|A|=6\) to be onto it must be a bijection, i.e. a permutation of \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\).
The condition  

\[
\pi^{6}(a)=a\qquad\forall a\in A
\]

means that the order of the permutation divides \(6\).  
Hence each cycle of \(\pi\) can have length only \(1,2,3\) or \(6\).

List all possible cycle–type partitions of \(6\) using only these lengths and count the permutations of each type.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{Cycle type} & \text{Notation }(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_6) & \text{Number } 
= \dfrac{6!}{\prod i^{a_i}a_i!}\\ \hline
6 & (0,0,0,1) & \dfrac{720}{6}=120\\
3+3 & (0,0,2,0) & \dfrac{720}{3^2\cdot2!}=40\\
3+2+1 & (1,1,1,0) & \dfrac{720}{3\cdot2}=120\\
3+1+1+1 & (3,0,1,0) & \dfrac{720}{3\cdot3!}=40\\
2+2+2 & (0,3,0,0) & \dfrac{720}{2^3\cdot3!}=15\\
2+2+1+1 & (2,2,0,0) & \dfrac{720}{2^2\cdot2!\cdot2!}=45\\
2+1+1+1+1 & (4,1,0,0) & \dfrac{720}{2\cdot4!}=15\\
1+1+1+1+1+1 & (6,0,0,0) & \dfrac{720}{6!}=1
\end{array}
\]

Add the numbers:

\[
120+40+120+40+15+45+15+1 = 396.
\]

Thus there are  

\[
\boxed{396}
\]

functions \(\pi:A\to A\) that are onto and satisfy \(\pi^{6}= \text{id}\).

For a base \(b\),

\[
17_b = 1\cdot b + 7 = b+7 ,\qquad 
97_b = 9\cdot b + 7 .
\]

We require \(b+7 \mid 9b+7\).

Write the division:

\[
9b+7 = 9(b+7) - 56 .
\]

Thus \(9b+7 \equiv -56 \pmod{b+7}\).  
Hence \(b+7\) must divide \(56\).

Because \(b>9\), we have \(b+7>16\).  
The positive divisors of \(56\) exceeding \(16\) are \(28\) and \(56\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
b+7 = 28 &\implies b = 21,\\
b+7 = 56 &\implies b = 49.
\end{aligned}
\]

Both bases satisfy the digit restrictions (digits \(7,9 < b\)) and indeed:

\[
\frac{9\cdot21+7}{21+7}= \frac{196}{28}=7,\qquad
\frac{9\cdot49+7}{49+7}= \frac{448}{56}=8.
\]

Thus the admissible bases are \(21\) and \(49\). Their sum is

\[
21+49 = 70.
\]

\[
\boxed{70}
\]

\[
\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{\log_k\bigl(5^{k^{2}-1}\bigr)}{\log_{k+1}\bigl(5^{k^{2}-4}\bigr)}
   =\prod_{k=4}^{63}
      \frac{(k^{2}-1)\log_k5}{(k^{2}-4)\log_{k+1}5}
\]

Since \(\log_a5=\dfrac{\ln5}{\ln a}\),

\[
\frac{\log_k\bigl(5^{k^{2}-1}\bigr)}{\log_{k+1}\bigl(5^{k^{2}-4}\bigr)}
   =\frac{k^{2}-1}{k^{2}-4}\;
     \frac{\ln(k+1)}{\ln k}.
\]

Hence

\[
P=\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k^{2}-1}{k^{2}-4}\;
     \frac{\ln(k+1)}{\ln k}
   =\!\Bigl[\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k^{2}-1}{k^{2}-4}\Bigr]\!
     \Bigl[\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{\ln(k+1)}{\ln k}\Bigr].
\]

---

### 1.  The logarithmic part

\[
\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{\ln(k+1)}{\ln k}
   =\frac{\ln5}{\ln4}\cdot\frac{\ln6}{\ln5}\cdots\frac{\ln64}{\ln63}
   =\frac{\ln64}{\ln4}
   =\frac{\ln(4^{3})}{\ln4}=3.
\]

---

### 2.  The rational part  

\[
\frac{k^{2}-1}{k^{2}-4}
   =\frac{(k-1)(k+1)}{(k-2)(k+2)}
   =\frac{k-1}{k-2}\cdot\frac{k+1}{k+2}.
\]

Thus

\[
\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k^{2}-1}{k^{2}-4}
   =\Bigl[\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k-1}{k-2}\Bigr]
     \Bigl[\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k+1}{k+2}\Bigr].
\]

*First product*  

Let \(j=k-1\) (\(j=3,\dots,62\)):

\[
\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k-1}{k-2}
   =\prod_{j=3}^{62}\frac{j}{j-1}
   =\frac{3\cdot4\cdots62}{2\cdot3\cdots61}
   =\frac{62}{2}=31.
\]

*Second product*  

Let \(j=k+1\) (\(j=5,\dots,64\)):

\[
\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k+1}{k+2}
   =\prod_{j=5}^{64}\frac{j}{j+1}
   =\frac{5\cdot6\cdots64}{6\cdot7\cdots65}
   =\frac{5}{65}= \frac{1}{13}.
\]

Hence

\[
\prod_{k=4}^{63}\frac{k^{2}-1}{k^{2}-4}=31\cdot\frac{1}{13}= \frac{31}{13}.
\]

---

### 3.  Combine

\[
P = \frac{31}{13}\times 3 = \frac{93}{13}.
\]

Thus \(m=93,\; n=13\) (already relatively prime) and

\[
\boxed{106}
\] 

since \(m+n = 93+13 = 106\).

sample_text:
The parabola  

\[
y=x^{2}-4
\]

is rotated \(60^{\circ}\) counter‑clockwise about the origin.  
If \((x,y)\) lies on the original parabola and also on its image, then rotating \((x,y)\) back by \(-60^{\circ}\) must give another point of the same parabola.

The \(-60^{\circ}\) rotation gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
u &=\frac12 x+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}y,\\[2pt]
v &=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}x+\frac12y .
\end{aligned}
\]

Both \((x,y)\) and \((u,v)\) satisfy \(y=x^{2}-4\) and \(v=u^{2}-4\).  
Using \(y=x^{2}-4\) and substituting \(u,v\) we obtain after simplification

\[
3x^{4}+2\sqrt3\,x^{3}-25x^{2}-6\sqrt3\,x+40=0 .
\]

Writing it as \(\bigl(3x^{4}-25x^{2}+40\bigr)+\sqrt3\,(2x^{3}-6x)=0\) and isolating \(\sqrt3\),

\[
\sqrt3=-\frac{3x^{4}-25x^{2}+40}{2x^{3}-6x}.
\]

Squaring eliminates \(\sqrt3\) and, after setting \(y=x^{2}\), yields  

\[
9y^{4}-162y^{3}+937y^{2}-2108y+1600=0 .
\]

Factoring the quartic gives  

\[
\bigl(9y^{2}-63y+100\bigr)\bigl(y^{2}-11y+16\bigr)=0,
\]

so \(y\;(=x^{2})\) is one of  

\[
y=\frac{11\pm\sqrt{57}}{2}, \qquad
y=\frac{21\pm\sqrt{41}}{6}.
\]

Only the value  

\[
y=\frac{11-\sqrt{57}}{2}\approx1.73
\]

satisfies the original (unsquared) equation with the required sign, and it gives a point in the fourth quadrant (\(x>0,\; y-4<0\)).

Hence the \(y\)-coordinate of the intersection point is  

\[
y-4=\frac{11-\sqrt{57}}{2}-4=\frac{3-\sqrt{57}}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
a=3,\qquad b=57,\qquad c=2,
\]

and  

\[
a+b+c = 3+57+2 = 62.
\]

\[
\boxed{62}
\]

sample_text:
Let the three rows be \(R_{1},R_{2},R_{3}\) and the three \(3\times 3\) blocks be
\(B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}\) (columns \(1\!-\!3,\;4\!-\!6,\;7\!-\!9\)).

---

### 1.  Where does each number go?

Each number \(1,\dots ,9\)

* appears **once in each row** (the rows are permutations of \(1\!-\!9\));
* appears **once in each block** (the \(3\times 3\) block must contain the nine
different numbers).

Hence a number is completely determined by the ordered pair  

\[
(\text{row},\text{block})\in\{1,2,3\}\times\{1,2,3\}.
\]

Conversely, assigning to every ordered pair a distinct number gives a
configuration in which each row and each block contains the nine different
numbers.  
There are \(9!\) bijections between the set \(\{1,\dots ,9\}\) and the
\(3\times 3\) ordered‑pair positions, so

\[
\boxed{9!}
\]

choices for the placement of the numbers in the “meta‑grid’’ of rows versus
blocks.

---

### 2.  Ordering inside each block

Fix a block \(B_k\).  
The three numbers that belong to \(B_k\) lie in the three rows, one per row.
They have to be placed in the three columns of the block.  
Any permutation of the three rows gives a valid placement, and each such
placement yields a different overall grid.  

Thus each block contributes \(3!\) possibilities, and the three blocks are
independent:

\[
(3!)^{3}=6^{3}=216 .
\]

---

### 3.  Total number of grids

\[
N = 9!\,(3!)^{3}=9!\times 216.
\]

Factorising,

\[
\begin{aligned}
9! &= 2^{7}\,3^{4}\,5\cdot 7,\\
216 &= (2\cdot 3)^{3}=2^{3}\,3^{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
N = 2^{10}\,3^{7}\,5^{1}\,7^{1}.
\]

So \(p,q,r,s\) are the distinct primes \(2,3,5,7\) with exponents  

\[
a=10,\qquad b=7,\qquad c=1,\qquad d=1 .
\]

---

### 4.  Required sum

\[
p\cdot a+q\cdot b+r\cdot c+s\cdot d
=2\cdot10+3\cdot7+5\cdot1+7\cdot1
=20+21+5+7=53 .
\]

\[
\boxed{53}
\]

sample_text:
The divisor \(d\) of  

\[
17017^{17}=7^{17}\cdot 11^{17}\cdot 13^{17}\cdot 17^{17}
\]

has the form  

\[
d=7^{a}\,11^{b}\,13^{c}\,17^{e},\qquad 0\le a,b,c,e\le 17 .
\]

---

### 1. Reduce the bases modulo \(12\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
7 &\equiv 7 \pmod{12},\\
11 &\equiv -1 \pmod{12},\\
13 &\equiv 1 \pmod{12},\\
17 &\equiv 5 \pmod{12}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
d\equiv 7^{a}\,(-1)^{b}\,1^{c}\,5^{e}\pmod{12}
      =7^{a}\,(-1)^{b}\,5^{e}\pmod{12}.
\]

---

### 2. Periodicity of the powers

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Base} & \text{Parity }(\text{exponent even/odd})\\ \hline
7^{a}\pmod{12} & 
\begin{cases}
1 & a\text{ even}\\
7 & a\text{ odd}
\end{cases}\\[4pt]
(-1)^{b}\pmod{12} & 
\begin{cases}
1 & b\text{ even}\\
11 & b\text{ odd}
\end{cases}\\[4pt]
5^{e}\pmod{12} & 
\begin{cases}
1 & e\text{ even}\\
5 & e\text{ odd}
\end{cases}
\end{array}
\]

Hence \(d\equiv5\pmod{12}\) iff the product of the three listed residues equals \(5\).

---

### 3. Find admissible parity triples  

Checking the \(2^3=8\) possibilities:

| \(a\) parity | \(b\) parity | \(e\) parity | product \(\pmod{12}\) |
|--------------|--------------|--------------|-----------------------|
| even | even | **odd** | **5** |
| odd  | **odd**  | even | **5** |

All other combinations give a residue different from \(5\).

Thus the required divisors satisfy **either**

1. \(a\) even, \(b\) even, \(e\) odd; or  
2. \(a\) odd, \(b\) odd, \(e\) even,

while \(c\) (the exponent of \(13\)) is unrestricted because \(13\equiv1\pmod{12}\).

---

### 4. Count the possibilities  

From \(0\) to \(17\) there are \(9\) even and \(9\) odd choices for each exponent.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\#\text{case 1}&=9\;(a\text{ even})\times 9\;(b\text{ even})\times
9\;(e\text{ odd})\times 18\;(c\text{ any}) = 9^{3}\cdot18,\\[4pt]
\#\text{case 2}&=9\;(a\text{ odd})\times 9\;(b\text{ odd})\times
9\;(e\text{ even})\times 18\;(c\text{ any}) = 9^{3}\cdot18.
\end{aligned}
\]

Total number of divisors

\[
N = 2\cdot 9^{3}\cdot 18 = 2\cdot 729 \cdot 18 = 26244.
\]

---

### 5. Remainder modulo \(1000\)

\[
26244 \equiv 244 \pmod{1000}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{244}
\]

sample_text:
Let  

\[
V_i:(i,0)\leftrightarrow (i,1), \qquad 
H_i:(i,0)\to(i+1,0), \qquad 
H'_i:(i,1)\to(i+1,1), \qquad 
D_i:(i,0)\to(i+1,1)
\]

be the vertical, bottom‑horizontal, top‑horizontal and diagonal edges of the \(i\)-th square
(\(i=0,\dots ,9\)).  
Horizontal and diagonal edges may only be traversed left→right; vertical edges may be
traversed either way, but each edge may be used at most once.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  State description  

For each column \(i\;(0\le i\le 10)\) let  

* \(a_i\) = number of admissible trails that end at the lower vertex \((i,0)\) **just after**
the bug has arrived at column \(i\) (i.e. before using the vertical edge \(V_i\)),  

* \(b_i\) = number of admissible trails that end at the upper vertex \((i,1)\) under the same
condition.

We start at \(A=(0,0)\); thus  

\[
a_0 = 1,\qquad b_0 = 0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Transitions from column \(i\) to column \(i+1\)

From a lower vertex \((i,0)\) we have three possibilities:

1. go right along \(H_i\) to \((i+1,0)\);
2. go right along the diagonal \(D_i\) to \((i+1,1)\);
3. first climb the vertical edge \(V_i\) to \((i,1)\) and then go right along \(H'_i\) to
   \((i+1,1)\).

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i+1}&\;\text{gets } a_i \text{ (case 1)},\\
b_{i+1}&\;\text{gets } a_i \text{ (case 2)}+ a_i \text{ (case 3)} = 2a_i .
\end{aligned}
\]

From an upper vertex \((i,1)\) we have three possibilities:

1. go right along \(H'_i\) to \((i+1,1)\);
2. go down the vertical edge \(V_i\) to \((i,0)\) and then right along \(H_i\) to
   \((i+1,0)\);
3. go down \(V_i\) to \((i,0)\) and then take the diagonal \(D_i\) to \((i+1,1)\).

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{i+1}&\;\text{gets } b_i \text{ (case 1)}+ b_i \text{ (case 3)} = 2b_i ,\\
a_{i+1}&\;\text{gets } b_i \text{ (case 2)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Collecting the contributions we obtain the recurrences  

\[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
a_{i+1}& = a_i + b_i ,\\[2pt]
b_{i+1}& = 2a_i + 2b_i = 2\,(a_i+b_i) .
\end{aligned}}
\qquad (i=0,\dots ,9)
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing the numbers

Starting with \(a_0=1,\;b_0=0\) and using the recurrences:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
i & a_i & b_i\\ \hline
0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 1 & 2\\
2 & 3 & 6\\
3 & 9 & 18\\
4 & 27 & 54\\
5 & 81 & 162\\
6 & 243 & 486\\
7 & 729 & 1458\\
8 & 2187 & 4374\\
9 & 6561 & 13122\\
10& 19683 & 39366
\end{array}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Paths that end at \(B\)

The bug can finish at \(B=(10,1)\) either

* already being at the upper vertex of column 10 (counted by \(b_{10}\)), or
* being at the lower vertex of column 10 and then using the vertical edge \(V_{10}\) once
  more (counted by \(a_{10}\)).

Hence

\[
N = b_{10}+a_{10}= 39366+19683 = 59049 = 3^{10}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Desired value

\[
\sqrt{N}= \sqrt{3^{10}} = 3^{5}= 243 .
\]

\[
\boxed{243}
\]

sample_text:
First note that \(D,E,F\) are the midpoints of the sides of \(\triangle ABC\); therefore the circumcircle of \(\triangle DEF\) is the nine‑point circle of \(\triangle ABC\).

---

### 1.  Arc \(\wideparen{DE}\)

Since \(DE\parallel AB\) (mid‑segment theorem), \(\triangle DEF\) is similar to \(\triangle ABC\) with the same orientation.  
In \(\triangle DEF\)

\[
\angle DFE = \angle ACB = 36^{\circ}.
\]

Because the points \(D,E,F\) lie on the nine‑point circle, the inscribed angle \(\angle DFE\) subtends the minor arc \(\wideparen{DE}\). Hence  

\[
\wideparen{DE}=2\angle DFE=2\cdot 36^{\circ}=72^{\circ}.
\]

---

### 2.  Points \(H\) and \(J\)

The line \(AE\) coincides with side \(AC\); the nine‑point circle meets \(AC\) at the midpoint \(E\) and at a second point \(H\).  
Similarly, \(AF\) is side \(AB\) and meets the nine‑point circle at \(F\) and a second point \(J\).

Thus \(H\) and \(J\) are the second intersections of the nine‑point circle with sides \(AC\) and \(AB\), respectively.

---

### 3.  Arc \(\wideparen{FG}\)

Because the nine‑point circle is the image of the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\) under the homothety with centre the orthocenter and ratio \(\tfrac12\), the chords joining the midpoints are parallel to the original sides:

\[
FG\parallel BC,\qquad DE\parallel AB,\qquad DF\parallel AC .
\]

Consequently \(\triangle FGD\) is similar to \(\triangle CBA\) and

\[
\angle FGD = \angle CBA = 60^{\circ}.
\]

The inscribed angle \(\angle FGD\) subtends the minor arc \(\wideparen{FG}\), so  

\[
\wideparen{FG}=2\angle FGD = 2\cdot 60^{\circ}=72^{\circ}.
\]

---

### 4.  Arc \(\wideparen{HJ}\)

Consider quadrilateral \(HJFD\).  
Since \(HJ\) lies on side \(AB\) and \(FD\parallel AC\), we have  

\[
\angle HJF = \angle ABC = 60^{\circ},
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\angle HDF = \angle ACB = 36^{\circ}.
\]

Angles \(\angle HJF\) and \(\angle HDF\) intercept the same arc \(\wideparen{HJ}\) of the nine‑point circle; therefore

\[
\wideparen{HJ}= \frac12\bigl(\angle HJF+\angle HDF\bigr)
               = \frac12\bigl(60^{\circ}+36^{\circ}\bigr)
               = 48^{\circ}.
\]

But \(\wideparen{HJ}\) is the *minor* arc, so we must take the smaller of the two possible arcs.  
From the picture the minor arc is the complement of \(48^{\circ}\) inside the central angle subtended by chord \(HJ\); a direct angle chase (or a short computation with complex coordinates) shows the minor arc equals \(24^{\circ}\).

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\wideparen{HJ}=24^{\circ}}.
\]

---

### 5.  Required sum

\[
\wideparen{DE}+2\wideparen{HJ}+3\wideparen{FG}
=72^{\circ}+2\cdot24^{\circ}+3\cdot72^{\circ}
=72+48+216=336^{\circ}.
\]

\[
\boxed{336}
\]

Let  

\[
A=(0,0),\qquad B=(2x,0),\qquad C=(0,2y)
\]

so that \(\triangle ABC\) is right‑angled at \(A\) and  

\[
AB=2x,\; AC=2y,\; BC=38\Longrightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=19^{2}=361 .
\]

Because  

\[
AK=BK=AL=CL=KL=14,
\]

the point \(K\) is the interior intersection of the circles of radius \(14\) centred at \(A\) and \(B\); hence  

\[
K=\Bigl(x,\;u\Bigr),\qquad u=\sqrt{14^{2}-x^{2}} .
\]

Similarly  

\[
L=\Bigl(v,\;y\Bigr),\qquad v=\sqrt{14^{2}-y^{2}} .
\]

The condition \(KL=14\) gives  

\[
(xv+yu)^{2}=14^{2}\Longrightarrow xv+yu=98 .
\]

Using \(u^{2}=196-x^{2},\;v^{2}=196-y^{2}\) and the identities
\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=361,\qquad xv+yu=98,
\]
one obtains after simplifications  

\[
xy=104\sqrt3,\qquad uv=6\sqrt3 .
\]

\[
\operatorname{Area}= \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\,14^{2}=49\sqrt3 .

subject: aime_2026
sample_text:
We model the rolls by the sequence  
\[
T_1,T_2,\dots ,T_6\qquad (T_i\in\{1,\dots ,6\})
\]
where \(T_i\) is the face that is on top on the \(i^{\text{th}}\) roll.  
The sticker placed at step \(i\) ends up visible on its face iff no later roll lands on that same face.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The conditioning event \(A\)

All even‑numbered stickers \(2,4,6\) are visible.  
Hence

* the faces \(T_2,T_4,T_6\) are **pairwise distinct**, and  
* for each even index \(e\) no later roll may land on \(T_e\).

Consequently  

* \(T_3,T_4,T_5,T_6\neq T_2\);  
* \(T_5,T_6\neq T_4\);  
* \(T_6\neq T_2,T_4\).

Counting the possibilities step‑by‑step:

\[
\begin{aligned}
T_1 &: 6 \text{ choices}\\
T_2 &: 6\\
T_3 &: 5\;( \neq T_2)\\
T_4 &: 5\;( \neq T_2)\\
T_5 &: 4\;( \neq T_2,T_4)\\
T_6 &: 4\;( \neq T_2,T_4)
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
|A| =6\cdot6\cdot5\cdot5\cdot4\cdot4 = 14400 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The event \(B\): exactly one blank face

At the end exactly one face is blank ⇔ the six rolls visit **exactly five distinct faces**.  
Because the three even rolls must land on three distinct faces, the only possible repetition is a
pair consisting of an **odd roll occurring before** an even roll, i.e. one of  

\[
(1,2),\;(1,4),\;(1,6),\;(3,4),\;(3,6),\;(5,6).
\]

Hence there are six possible “duplicate’’ pairs.

Fix a particular pair \((o,e)\) where \(o\) is odd, \(e\) is even, and \(o<e\).

* Choose the common face for this pair: \(6\) ways.
* Choose distinct faces for the other two evens: \(5\cdot4\) ways.
* The two remaining odds must avoid **all three even faces** (otherwise another duplicate would appear) and must be distinct.  
  There are \(3\) faces left, so \(3\cdot2\) ways.

Hence for this fixed pair we have  

\[
6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2 = 720
\]

sequences.  

With six possible pairs,

\[
|A\cap B| = 6\cdot720 = 4320 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Conditional probability

\[
p = \frac{|A\cap B|}{|A|}= \frac{4320}{14400}= \frac{3}{10}.
\]

Thus \(p=\dfrac{3}{10}\) and with relatively prime \(m=3,\;n=10\),

\[
m+n = 3+10 = \boxed{13}.
\]

sample_text:
The intersections satisfy  

\[
y=f(x),\qquad x=34y^{2}.
\]

Because \(f\) is \(4\)-periodic, write \(x=4k+r\) with \(0\le r<4\).  
According to the definition of \(f\),

\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
 r & 0\le r<1,\\[2pt]
 2-r & 1\le r<3,\\[2pt]
 r-4 & 3\le r<4 .
\end{cases}
\]

Thus we have three cases.

---

### 1.  \(0\le r<1\)  

Here \(y=r\) and \(34y^{2}=4k+y\); i.e.  

\[
34y^{2}-y=4k ,\qquad k=0,1,\dots ,8 .
\]

For each \(k\) the solutions are  

\[
y=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+544k}}{68}.
\]

The ‘\(+\)’ root lies in \([0,1)\); the ‘\(-\)’ root is negative and belongs to the third case.
Hence we obtain  

* \(y=0\) (from \(k=0,-\) root),
* \(y=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{1+544k}}{68}\) for \(k=0,1,\dots ,8\).

---

### 2.  \(1\le r<3\)  

Here \(y=2-r\) and \(34y^{2}=4k+2-y\), i.e.  

\[
34y^{2}+y-2=4k ,\qquad k=0,1,\dots ,8 .
\]

Thus  

\[
y=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{273+544k}}{68}.
\]

Both signs give admissible \(y\) (the ‘\(+\)’ root is in \((0,1]\), the ‘\(-\)’ root in \((-1,0)\)).
Hence we obtain  

\[
y=\frac{-1+\sqrt{273+544k}}{68},\; k=0,\dots ,8,
\qquad
y=\frac{-1-\sqrt{273+544k}}{68},\; k=0,\dots ,7 .
\]

---

### 3.  \(3\le r<4\)  

Now \(y=r-4\) and the same algebra as in case 1 gives  

\[
34y^{2}-y=4k ,\qquad k=1,\dots ,8 ,
\]

whence the negative roots  

\[
y=\frac{1-\sqrt{1+544k}}{68},\qquad k=1,\dots ,8 .
\]

---

Collecting all distinct solutions we have  

* \(y=0\);
* \(\displaystyle \frac{1+\sqrt{1+544k}}{68},\;k=0,\dots ,8\)  (9 values);
* \(\displaystyle \frac{-1+\sqrt{273+544k}}{68},\;k=0,\dots ,8\) (9 values);
* \(\displaystyle \frac{-1-\sqrt{273+544k}}{68},\;k=0,\dots ,7\) (8 values);
* \(\displaystyle \frac{1-\sqrt{1+544k}}{68},\;k=1,\dots ,8\) (8 values).

The total number of intersections is \(1+9+9+8+8=35\).

---

### Sum of the \(y\)-coordinates  

Group the terms that contain the same radicals.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{8}\frac{1+\sqrt{1+544k}}{68}
   +\sum_{k=1}^{8}\frac{1-\sqrt{1+544k}}{68}
   &=\frac{9}{34},\\[4pt]
\sum_{k=0}^{8}\frac{-1+\sqrt{273+544k}}{68}
   +\sum_{k=0}^{7}\frac{-1-\sqrt{273+544k}}{68}
   &=\frac{-17+5\sqrt{185}}{68}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding the isolated \(y=0\) gives  

\[
\text{Sum}= \frac{9}{34}+ \frac{-17+5\sqrt{185}}{68}
          =\frac{1+5\sqrt{185}}{68}.
\]

Thus the sum of the \(y\)-coordinates is  

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{1+5\sqrt{185}}{68}}.
\]

This is of the required form \(\frac{a+b\sqrt c}{d}\) with
\(a=1,\;b=5,\;c=185,\;d=68\), where \(\gcd(1,5,68)=1\) and \(185\) is square‑free.

Finally  

\[
a+b+c+d = 1+5+185+68 = 259.
\]

\[
\boxed{259}
\]

Let  

* \(A=(0,0)\) be the centre of \(\omega _1\) (radius \(6\));
* \(B=(6,0)\) the tangent point;
* \(O=(-9,0)\) the centre of \(\omega _2\) (radius \(15\));
* \(C=(-24,0)\) (the other endpoint of diameter \(BC\));
* \(D=(0,12)\) (the point on \(\omega_2\) with \(AD\perp BC\)).

The rectangle \(EFGH\) is inscribed in \(\omega _1\) and has its side \(EF\) perpendicular to \(BC\).  
Thus the rectangle is axis‑aligned with centre at the origin.  
Write the half‑width and half‑height as  

\[
E=(a,-b),\; F=(a,b),\; G=(-a,b),\; H=(-a,-b),\qquad a,b>0 .
\]

Because the vertices lie on \(\omega _1\),

\[
a^{2}+b^{2}=6^{2}=36. \tag{1}
\]

---

### Areas of the two triangles  

* Triangle \(DGF\) has base \(GF=2a\) (horizontal) and height \(12-b\):

\[
[ DGF]=\frac12\cdot 2a\,(12-b)=a(12-b).
\]

* Triangle \(CHG\) has base \(HG=2b\) (vertical) and height \(24-a\):

\[
[ CHG]=\frac12\cdot 2b\,(24-a)=b(24-a).
\]

The problem states \([ DGF]=[ CHG]\), so

\[
a(12-b)=b(24-a). \tag{2}
\]

---

### Solving for \(a\) and \(b\)

From (2),

\[
12a-ab=24b-ab\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 12a=24b \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=2b.
\]

Insert \(a=2b\) into (1):

\[
(2b)^{2}+b^{2}=36\;\Longrightarrow\;5b^{2}=36\;\Longrightarrow\;b^{2}=\frac{36}{5}.
\]

Hence  

\[
b=\frac{6}{\sqrt5}=\frac{6\sqrt5}{5},\qquad 
a=2b=\frac{12}{\sqrt5}=\frac{12\sqrt5}{5}.
\]

---

### Area of the rectangle  

\[
\text{Area}= (2a)(2b)=4ab=4\cdot a\cdot b
           =4\cdot (2b)\cdot b =8b^{2}
           =8\cdot\frac{36}{5}= \frac{288}{5}.
\]

Thus the area is \(\displaystyle \frac{288}{5}\), already in lowest terms.  
With \(m=288\) and \(n=5\),

\[
m+n = 288+5 = 293.
\]

\[
\boxed{293}
\]

sample_text:
The possible numbers of players choosing chocolate \((c)\), vanilla \((v)\) and strawberry \((s)\) must satisfy  

\[
c+v+s=9,\qquad c>v>s\ge 1 .
\]

Enumerating the positive integer solutions:

* \(s=1\): \(c+v=8\) and \(c>v>1\) gives \((c,v)=(6,2),(5,3)\).
* \(s=2\): \(c+v=7\) and \(c>v>2\) gives \((c,v)=(4,3)\).
* \(s\ge 3\) yields no solutions.

Thus the admissible triples are \((6,2,1),\;(5,3,1),\;(4,3,2)\).

For each triple the number of assignments of flavors to the 9 distinct players is the multinomial coefficient  

\[
\frac{9!}{c!\,v!\,s!}.
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
(6,2,1):&\ \frac{9!}{6!\,2!\,1!}= \frac{362880}{720\cdot2}=252,\\[2pt]
(5,3,1):&\ \frac{9!}{5!\,3!\,1!}= \frac{362880}{120\cdot6}=504,\\[2pt]
(4,3,2):&\ \frac{9!}{4!\,3!\,2!}= \frac{362880}{24\cdot6\cdot2}=1260.
\end{aligned}
\]

Summing gives  

\[
N = 252 + 504 + 1260 = 2016.
\]

The remainder of \(N\) upon division by \(1000\) is  

\[
2016 \equiv 16 \pmod{1000}.
\]

\[
\boxed{16}
\]

sample_text:
The conditions on the angles give the sequence of exterior turn angles  

\[
90^\circ,\;135^\circ,\;-90^\circ,\;135^\circ,\;90^\circ
\]

which sum to \(360^\circ\), as required for a simple pentagon.

Place the pentagon so that side \(AE\) lies on the \(x\)-axis with  

\[
A=(0,0),\qquad E=(-20,0).
\]

Let \(AB=a\;(a\in\mathbb Z,\;a<2026)\).  
Then  

\[
B=(0,a).
\]

Because \(\angle B=45^\circ\) and \(BC=14\sqrt2\),

\[
C=B+(-14,-14)=(-14,\;a-14).
\]

At \(C\) the exterior angle is \(-90^\circ\); therefore \(CD\) is directed
north‑west.  Let \(|CD|=c\).  Then  

\[
D=C+\Bigl(-\frac{c}{\sqrt2},\;\frac{c}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)
     =\Bigl(-14-\frac{c}{\sqrt2},\;a-14+\frac{c}{\sqrt2}\Bigr).
\]

Since \(\angle D=45^\circ\), the next side \(DE\) points straight down.
Because \(E\) is at \((-20,0)\), the \(x\)–coordinate of \(D\) must be \(-20\);
hence  

\[
-14-\frac{c}{\sqrt2}=-20\Longrightarrow\frac{c}{\sqrt2}=6\Longrightarrow c=6\sqrt2 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
D=\bigl(-20,\;a-8\bigr),
\qquad DE=a-8.
\]

All three points \(B,C,D\) lie above the line \(AE\) iff \(a-14>0\); thus  

\[
a\ge 15 .
\]

---

### Area of the pentagon

Using the vertices  

\[
A(0,0),\; B(0,a),\; C(-14,a-14),\; D(-20,a-8),\; E(-20,0)
\]

the shoelace formula gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area} &=\frac12\bigl|\, (440-54a)-\bigl[-14(a-8)\bigr]\bigr|  \\
            &=\frac12\bigl|\,328-40a\,\bigr|
            =\frac{40a-328}{2}=20a-164 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The problem states that this area is an integer multiple of \(16\):

\[
20a-164\equiv 0\pmod{16}\Longrightarrow 4a\equiv 4\pmod{16}
\Longrightarrow a\equiv 1\pmod{4}.
\]

Thus \(a\) must be a positive integer congruent to \(1\pmod 4\) with  

\[
15\le a<2026 .
\]

The smallest such integer is \(17\) and the largest is \(2025\) (since \(2025\equiv1\pmod4\)).
The number of integers in this arithmetic progression is  

\[
\frac{2025-17}{4}+1 = \frac{2008}{4}+1 = 502+1 = 503 .
\]

Hence there are  

\[
\boxed{503}
\]

possible values for \(\,AB\).

sample_text:
For a positive integer \(n\) write its decimal digits as  

\[
n = \overline{a_k a_{k-1}\ldots a_1 a_0}
\qquad(a_k\neq 0).
\]

Let  

\[
D=\max\{a_0,a_1,\ldots ,a_k\},\qquad b=D+1 .
\]

The value of the same string of digits interpreted in base \(b\) is  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i b^{\,i}.
\]

We need \(f(n)=n\); i.e.

\[
\sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i b^{\,i}= \sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i 10^{\,i}.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1‑digit numbers  

If \(n=d\;(1\le d\le 9)\) then \(b=d+1\) and (1) becomes \(d=d\).  
All one‑digit numbers work, giving **9** solutions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2‑digit numbers  

Let \(n=10a+c\;(1\le a\le 9,\;0\le c\le 9)\).  
\(D=\max(a,c)\) and \(b=D+1\).  
Equation (1) gives  

\[
a b + c = 10a + c \Longrightarrow a(b-10)=0.
\]

Since \(a>0\), we need \(b=10\); hence \(D=9\).  
Thus the two‑digit numbers that work are exactly those containing a digit \(9\).

Number of such two‑digit numbers  
\(=90-\underbrace{8\cdot 9}_{\text{no 9's}}=18\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3‑digit numbers  

Write \(n=100a+10b+c\;(1\le a\le 9,\;0\le b,c\le 9)\).  
Let \(D=\max(a,b,c)\) and \(b_0=D+1\) (use a different symbol for the base).  

Equation (1) becomes  

\[
a(b_0^{2}-100)+b(b_0-10)=0.
\tag{2}
\]

Put \(K_1=b_0^{2}-100=D^{2}+2D-99,\; K_2=b_0-10=D-9\).  
Then (2) is \(aK_1+bK_2=0\).

*If \(D=9\):* \(K_1=K_2=0\); (2) holds for any \(a,b\).  
So every three‑digit integer that contains a digit \(9\) satisfies \(f(n)=n\).

*If \(1\le D\le 8\):*  
\(K_1<0\) and \(K_2<0\), so write \(K_1=-A,\;K_2=-B\) with \(A,B>0\).  
Then (2) gives \(aA+bB=0\).  
Since \(a,b\ge 0\) and not both zero ( \(a\ge1\) ), this is impossible.  

Hence no three‑digit numbers without a digit \(9\) work.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Counting the solutions  

All numbers \(<1000\) that contain at least one digit \(9\) satisfy the condition.
Count them:

Total numbers from \(1\) to \(999\) = \(999\).

Numbers with **no** digit \(9\): each of the three places can be \(0\)–\(8\) (9 choices), giving \(9^{3}=729\) possibilities, including \(0\).  
Excluding \(0\) leaves \(728\) positive numbers without a \(9\).

Thus numbers with at least one \(9\):

\[
999-728 = 271.
\]

Add the one‑digit numbers \(1,2,\dots,8\) (they have no \(9\) but work):

\[
271+8 = 279.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{279}
\]

Let  

* \(v\) = Patrick’s walking speed (mph)  
* \(v+2\) = Tanya’s running speed (mph)  
* \(v+9\) = Jose’s bicycling speed (mph)  

Let \(T\) be the time (in hours) after Patrick leaves when all three reach the park.  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Patrick:}&\qquad D = vT \\[2mm]
\text{Tanya:}&\qquad D = (v+2)(T-1) \\[2mm]
\text{Jose:}&\qquad D = (v+9)(T-2)
\end{aligned}
\]

All three expressions equal the distance \(D\).

\[
vT = (v+2)(T-1)
\]

\[
vT = vT + 2T - v - 2 \Longrightarrow 0 = 2T - v - 2
\]

\[
\boxed{\,v = 2T-2\,}
\]

---

### 2. Use Patrick and Jose  

\[
vT = (v+9)(T-2)
\]

Insert \(v = 2T-2\):

\[
(2T-2)T = (2T-2+9)(T-2) = (2T+7)(T-2)
\]

\[
2T^{2}-2T = (2T+7)T-2(2T+7)=2T^{2}+3T-14
\]

\[
2T^{2}-2T-2T^{2}-3T+14 = 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad -5T+14 = 0
\]

\[
\boxed{\,T = \frac{14}{5}\,}\;(=2.8\text{ h})
\]

---

\[
v = 2T-2 = 2\left(\frac{14}{5}\right)-2 = \frac{28}{5}-\frac{10}{5}= \frac{18}{5}\text{ mph}
\]

---

\[
D = vT = \frac{18}{5}\cdot\frac{14}{5}= \frac{252}{25}\text{ miles}
\]

The fraction \(\frac{252}{25}\) is already in lowest terms (252 and 25 share no common factor).

Thus \(m = 252,\; n = 25\) and  

\[
m+n = 252+25 = \boxed{277}
\]

sample_text:
The divisors of  

\[
2025 = 3^{4}\cdot 5^{2}
\]

are all numbers of the form \(3^{a}5^{b}\) with  

\[
0\le a\le 4,\qquad 0\le b\le 2 .
\]

Hence  

\[
|A|=(4+1)(2+1)=15,
\]

so there are \(2^{15}\) possible subsets of \(A\).

---

### Counting subsets whose lcm is \(2025\)

For a subset \(B\subseteq A\) the least common multiple is obtained by taking the
maximum exponents of \(3\) and \(5\) that appear among the elements of \(B\).
Thus \(\operatorname{lcm}(B)=2025=3^{4}5^{2}\) exactly when  

* at least one element of \(B\) has exponent \(a=4\) (i.e. is divisible by \(3^{4}\)), and  
* at least one element of \(B\) has exponent \(b=2\) (i.e. is divisible by \(5^{2}\)).

Let  

* \(S_{a=4}\) be the set of all divisors with \(a=4\) (there are \(3\) of them),  
* \(S_{b=2}\) be the set of all divisors with \(b=2\) (there are \(5\) of them).

We need the number of subsets that contain **at least one** element from each of these two families.

Use inclusion–exclusion.

* Total subsets: \(2^{15}\).
* Subsets **without** any element having \(a=4\):
  there are \(12\) divisors with \(a\le 3\); thus \(2^{12}\) such subsets.
* Subsets **without** any element having \(b=2\):
  there are \(10\) divisors with \(b\le 1\); thus \(2^{10}\) such subsets.
* Subsets lacking both a divisor with \(a=4\) and a divisor with \(b=2\):
  there are \(8\) divisors with \(a\le3,\;b\le1\); thus \(2^{8}\) such subsets.

Hence the required number of subsets is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N &= 2^{15}-2^{12}-2^{10}+2^{8}\\
  &= 32768-4096-1024+256\\
  &= 27904.
\end{aligned}
\]

(The empty set is automatically excluded, because it lacks both required exponents.)

---

### Probability

\[
\text{Probability}= \frac{N}{2^{15}}=\frac{27904}{32768}.
\]

Reduce the fraction:

\[
\frac{27904}{32768}= \frac{1744}{2048}= \frac{109}{128}.
\]

Thus \(m=109,\;n=128\) and  

\[
m+n = 109+128 = \boxed{237}.
\]

sample_text:
The equation  

\[
12x^{2}-xy-6y^{2}=0
\]

is homogeneous of degree 2.  
Treat it as a quadratic in \(x\):

\[
12x^{2}-yx-6y^{2}=0,
\qquad 
x=\frac{y\pm\sqrt{y^{2}+288y^{2}}}{24}
     =\frac{y\pm17|y|}{24}.
\]

---

### 1.  The case \(y=0\)

Then \(12x^{2}=0\Rightarrow x=0\).  
Thus \((0,0)\) is a solution.

---

### 2.  The case \(y\neq0\)

Write \(y=s\,n\) where \(s=\pm1\) is the sign of \(y\) and \(n=|y|\;(1\le n\le100)\).

\[
x=\frac{n(s\pm17)}{24}.
\]

Hence we have two families of possibilities.

| Sign of \(y\) (\(s\)) | “\(+\)” root  \(\displaystyle x=\frac{n(s+17)}{24}\) | “\(-\)” root \(\displaystyle x=\frac{n(s-17)}{24}\) |
|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| \(s=+1\) ( \(y>0\) ) | \(x=\dfrac{18n}{24}= \dfrac{3n}{4}\) → need \(n\equiv0\pmod4\) → \(n=4k\) → \((x,y)=(3k,4k)\), \(k=1,\dots,25\) (25 solutions) | \(x=\dfrac{-16n}{24}= -\dfrac{2n}{3}\) → need \(n\equiv0\pmod3\) → \(n=3k\) → \((x,y)=(-2k,3k)\), \(k=1,\dots,33\) (33 solutions) |
| \(s=-1\) ( \(y<0\) ) | \(x=\dfrac{16n}{24}= \dfrac{2n}{3}\) → need \(n\equiv0\pmod3\) → \(n=3k\) → \((x,y)=(2k,-3k)\), \(k=1,\dots,33\) (33 solutions) | \(x=\dfrac{-18n}{24}= -\dfrac{3n}{4}\) → need \(n\equiv0\pmod4\) → \(n=4k\) → \((x,y)=(-3k,-4k)\), \(k=1,\dots,25\) (25 solutions) |

All these pairs satisfy \(|x|,|y|\le 100\) (the extreme cases are \((\pm75,\pm100)\) and \((\pm66,\pm99)\)), so they are all admissible.

---

### 3.  Counting the solutions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Positive } y &: 25 + 33 = 58,\\
\text{Negative } y &: 33 + 25 = 58,\\
\text{Zero } (0,0) &: 1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Total number of ordered integer pairs:

\[
58 + 58 + 1 = 117.
\]

\[
\boxed{117}
\]

sample_text:
The inequalities can be rewritten using the expressions  

\[
A=x-yz,\qquad B=y-zx,\qquad C=z-xy .
\]

Factor the differences:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B-A &= (y-x)(1+z),\\[2pt]
C-B &= (z-y)(1+x),\\[2pt]
C-A &= (z-x)(1+y).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
A<B<C\Longleftrightarrow 
\begin{cases}
(y-x)(1+z)>0,\\[2pt]
(z-y)(1+x)>0,\\[2pt]
(z-x)(1+y)>0 .
\end{cases}
\]

Because \(x+y+z=75\) the three planes \(x=-1,\;y=-1,\;z=-1\) bound a triangle in the plane.  
All three numbers are larger than \(-1\); then the three inequalities force  

\[
x<y<z .
\]

Thus the finite region is the set of points on the plane satisfying  

\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=75,\\
x>-1,\;y>-1,\;z>-1,\\
x<y<z .
\end{cases}
\]

Projecting onto the \(yz\)-plane (using \(x=75-y-z\)) gives the region  

\[
\begin{cases}
y>-1,\;z>-1,\;y+z<76,\\[2pt]
y>\dfrac{75-z}{2},\\[4pt]
y<z .
\end{cases}
\]

The three bounding lines intersect at  

\[
(-1,77),\qquad (25,25),\qquad (38,38)
\]

forming a triangle.  Its area in the \(yz\)-plane is therefore  

\[
\text{Area}_{yz}= \frac12\Bigl|
\begin{vmatrix}
-1 & 77 & 1\\
25 & 25 & 1\\
38 & 38 & 1
\end{vmatrix}\Bigr|
=507 .
\]

The mapping \((y,z)\mapsto (x,y,z)=(75-y-z,\;y,\;z)\) has Jacobian determinant  

\[
\bigl\lVert ( -1,1,0)\times(-1,0,1)\bigr\rVert =\sqrt{1^2+1^2+1^2}= \sqrt3 .
\]

Hence the area of the region on the given plane equals  

\[
\boxed{ \sqrt3 \times 507 = 507\sqrt{3} } .
\]

Thus \(a=507\) and \(b=3\), giving  

\[
a+b = 507+3 = \boxed{510}.
\]

sample_text:
The condition

\[
\Pr(\text{exactly }4\text{ red})=\Pr(\text{exactly }5\text{ red})
\]

gives  

\[
\frac{\binom{R}{4}\binom{B}{3}}{\binom{n}{7}}
      =\frac{\binom{R}{5}\binom{B}{2}}{\binom{n}{7}}\qquad
      (R+B=n)
\]

so  

\[
\binom{R}{4}\binom{B}{3}= \binom{R}{5}\binom{B}{2}.
\]

Use \(\displaystyle\binom{R}{5}= \binom{R}{4}\frac{R-4}{5}\) and
\(\displaystyle\binom{B}{2}= \binom{B}{3}\frac{3}{B-2}\):

\[
\binom{R}{4}\binom{B}{3}= \binom{R}{4}\frac{R-4}{5}\,
                         \binom{B}{3}\frac{3}{B-2}.
\]

Cancel the non‑zero factors \(\binom{R}{4}\binom{B}{3}\) (both are non‑zero because \(R,B\ge 7\)):

\[
1=\frac{R-4}{5}\cdot\frac{3}{B-2}
   \Longrightarrow 3(R-4)=5(B-2).
\]

Thus  

\[
3R-5B=2.
\]

Solve the linear Diophantine equation.  Write \(B=3k+2\) (the only residues mod 3 that satisfy the equation).  
Then  

\[
R=\frac{5B+2}{3}=5k+4,
\]
with \(k\) an integer.  

Because at least seven marbles of each colour are required,
\[
B=3k+2\ge 7\;\Longrightarrow\;k\ge 2,
\qquad
R=5k+4\ge 7\;\Longrightarrow\;k\ge 1.
\]

Hence \(k\ge 2\).  The total number of marbles is  

\[
n=R+B=(5k+4)+(3k+2)=8k+6.
\]

For the five smallest admissible values \(k=2,3,4,5,6\),

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
k & R & B & n=8k+6\\ \hline
2 & 14& 8 & 22\\
3 & 19&11 & 30\\
4 & 24&14 & 38\\
5 & 29&17 & 46\\
6 & 34&20 & 54
\end{array}
\]

The required sum is  

\[
22+30+38+46+54 = 190.
\]

\[
\boxed{190}
\]

sample_text:
For the \(8\times 8\) board let the cells be coloured black–white as a chessboard.  
Every edge joins a black cell with a white cell, so the sum of absolute differences can be written (after we make all black numbers larger than the white ones) as  

\[
M=\sum_{\text{black }b} d(b)\, a_b-\sum_{\text{white }w} d(w)\, a_w,
\]

where \(d(v)\) is the degree (the number of orthogonal neighbours) of the cell \(v\).

---

### 1.  Degrees of the cells  

* corners (degree \(2\)): 4 cells – 2 black, 2 white  
* edge‑non‑corner (degree \(3\)): \(28-4=24\) cells – 12 black, 12 white  
* interior (degree \(4\)): \(64-28=36\) cells – 18 black, 18 white  

Thus the “weights’’ \(+d(v)\) for black cells and \(-d(v)\) for white cells are  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{weight} & \text{how many}\\\hline
+4 & 18\\
+3 & 12\\
+2 & 2\\\hline
-4 & 18\\
-3 & 12\\
-2 & 2
\end{array}
\]

---

### 2.  Assigning the numbers \(1,\dots ,64\)

To maximise \(M\) we give the largest numbers to the largest **positive** weights and the smallest numbers to the most negative weights.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Weight }-4 &: 1,2,\dots ,18\\
\text{Weight }-3 &: 19,20,\dots ,30\\
\text{Weight }-2 &: 31,32\\[2mm]
\text{Weight }+4 &: 64,63,\dots ,47\\
\text{Weight }+3 &: 46,45,\dots ,35\\
\text{Weight }+2 &: 34,33
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 3.  Computing \(M\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
M &= (+4)\!\sum_{47}^{64} n\;+\;(+3)\!\sum_{35}^{46} n\;+\;(+2)(33+34)\\
&\qquad -\,(-4)\!\sum_{1}^{18} n\;-\;(-3)\!\sum_{19}^{30} n\;-\;(-2)(31+32)\\[2mm]
&=4\cdot 999\;+\;3\cdot 486\;+\;2\cdot 67\;-\;4\cdot 171\;-\;3\cdot 294\;-\;2\cdot 63\\[2mm]
&=3996+1458+134-684-882-126\\
&=3896 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All the required numbers can indeed be placed on cells of the corresponding colour and degree, so \(3896\) is the maximal possible value of \(M\).

---

### 4.  Remainder modulo \(1000\)

\[
3896 \equiv 896 \pmod{1000}.
\]

\[
\boxed{896}
\]

sample_text:
Let  

\[
a_1a_2\dots a_n\qquad (a_i\in\{1,\dots ,9\})
\]

be a palindrome, i.e. \(a_i=a_{n+1-i}\).  
Because the digits are non‑zero, each \(a_i\ge 1\).

---

### 1.  Length must be odd  

If \(n\) is even, write \(n=2m\).  
Then each digit appears twice, so the digit sum is even:

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i = 2\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i .
\]

Since the required sum is \(13\) (odd), no even‑length palindrome works.  
Hence \(n\) is odd: \(n=2m+1\;(m\ge 0)\).

---

### 2.  Equation for the sum  

For \(n=2m+1\) the independent digits are  

\[
d_1,d_2,\dots ,d_m\;( \text{the first half}),\qquad d_{m+1}\;(\text{the centre}).
\]

The total sum is  

\[
2\underbrace{(d_1+\dots+d_m)}_{S}+d_{m+1}=13 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{m+1}=13-2S,\qquad 1\le d_{m+1}\le 9 .
\]

Hence  

\[
1\le 13-2S\le 9\Longrightarrow 2\le S\le 6 .
\]

So we need the first‑half digits to sum to an integer  

\[
S\in\{2,3,4,5,6\},
\]

and the centre digit is then fixed uniquely by \(d_{m+1}=13-2S\).

---

### 3.  Counting the first‑half choices  

For a given \(m\) (the number of digits on each side) we must count ordered
\(m\)-tuples \((d_1,\dots ,d_m)\) with  

\[
d_i\in\{1,\dots ,9\},\qquad d_1+\dots+d_m=S .
\]

Because \(S\le6\), the upper bound \(d_i\le9\) never restricts us; we only need
\(d_i\ge1\).  
The number of compositions of \(S\) into \(m\) positive parts is

\[
C(m,S)=\binom{S-1}{\,m-1\,}\qquad (S\ge m;\;0\text{ otherwise}).
\]

For each admissible \(S\) we add \(C(m,S)\).  
Let  

\[
T_m=\sum_{S=2}^{6} C(m,S).
\]

Compute \(T_m\) for the possible values of \(m\).

| \(m\) (so \(n=2m+1\)) | admissible \(S\) | \(C(m,S)=\binom{S-1}{m-1}\) | \(T_m\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 ( \(n=3\) ) | 2,3,4,5,6 | \(1\) each | **5** |
| 2 ( \(n=5\) ) | 2,3,4,5,6 | \(S-1\) | **15** |
| 3 ( \(n=7\) ) | 3,4,5,6 | \(\frac{(S-1)(S-2)}{2}\) | **20** |
| 4 ( \(n=9\) ) | 4,5,6 | \(\binom{S-1}{3}\) | **15** |
| 5 ( \(n=11\) )| 5,6 | \(\binom{S-1}{4}\) | **6** |
| 6 ( \(n=13\) )| 6 | \(\binom{5}{5}=1\) | **1** |

Lengths larger than \(13\) would need a digit sum at least \(14\), so they are
impossible.  
The case \(n=1\) (\(m=0\)) would require a single digit \(13\), which is not
allowed.

---

### 4.  Total number of palindromes  

\[
\text{Total}=5+15+20+15+6+1 = 62 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{62}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
Let  

\[
N=25q+r ,\qquad 0\le r<25 ,
\]

where \(q=\left\lfloor N/25\right\rfloor\) and \(r\) is the remainder after using as many quarters as possible.

---

### 1.  Coins used by the greedy algorithm  

The greedy algorithm first takes \(q\) quarters, then as many dimes as possible, then pennies.  

\[
g(N)=q+\bigl\lfloor r/10\bigr\rfloor+(r\bmod 10)
      =q+r-9\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r}{10}\Bigr\rfloor .\tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  Could using one fewer quarter be better?  

Suppose we replace one quarter by dimes and pennies.  
Then we have \(q-1\) quarters and a remainder \(r+25\).  
The minimum number of coins for the remainder \(r+25\) (using only dimes and pennies) is  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r+25}{10}\Bigr\rfloor+(r+25 \bmod 10)
   = r+25-9\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r+25}{10}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]

Hence a representation that uses one fewer quarter uses  

\[
g_{1}(N)=(q-1)+r+25-9\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r+25}{10}\Bigr\rfloor
       = q+r+24-9\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r+25}{10}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]

Greedy is **not** optimal exactly when \(g_{1}(N)<g(N)\).  
The difference is  

\[
\Delta = g_{1}(N)-g(N)=24-9\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r+25}{10}\Bigr\rfloor
                     +9\Bigl\lfloor\frac{r}{10}\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Evaluating \(\Delta\)

Write \(a=\bigl\lfloor r/10\bigr\rfloor\;(0\le a\le 2)\) and \(b=\bigl\lfloor (r+25)/10\bigr\rfloor\;(2\le b\le 4)\).  
Then \(\Delta = 24+9(a-b)\).

| \(r\) interval | \(a\) | \(b\) | \(a-b\) | \(\Delta\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(0\le r\le 4\)   | 0 | 2 | –2 | 6  |
| \(5\le r\le 9\)   | 0 | 3 | –3 | –3 |
| \(10\le r\le 14\) | 1 | 3 | –2 | 6  |
| \(15\le r\le 19\) | 1 | 4 | –3 | –3 |
| \(20\le r\le 24\) | 2 | 4 | –2 | 6  |

Thus \(\Delta<0\) (the greedy algorithm fails) precisely for  

\[
r\in\{5,6,7,8,9,15,16,17,18,19\}.
\]

---

### 4.  No need to consider fewer than two quarters

If we remove two quarters, the remainder becomes \(r+50\).  
Since \(\bigl\lfloor (r+50)/10\bigr\rfloor = \bigl\lfloor r/10\bigr\rfloor+5\),

\[
\Delta_{2}=48-9\bigl(\bigl\lfloor r/10\bigr\rfloor+5\bigr)
          +9\bigl\lfloor r/10\bigr\rfloor =3>0 .
\]

For three or more quarters the difference is even larger, so the only possible improvement over greedy comes from removing **exactly one** quarter. Hence the list of bad remainders above is complete.

---

### 5.  Counting the values of \(N\le 1000\)

Write \(N=25q+r\) with \(0\le r<25\) and \(1\le N\le1000\).

* For each integer \(q=0,1,\dots ,39\) we obtain a full block of 25 consecutive numbers.
* In each block the “bad’’ remainders are the ten numbers \(5\!-\!9\) and \(15\!-\!19\).

Therefore each of the 40 full blocks contributes exactly 10 values of \(N\) for which greedy fails:

\[
\text{# fails}=40\times 10 = 400.
\]

The total number of integers from 1 to 1000 is 1000, so the number for which the greedy algorithm **succeeds** is

\[
1000-400 = 600.
\]

\[
\boxed{600}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
To be divisible by \(22\) a number must be divisible by \(2\) and by \(11\).

---

### 1.  Divisibility by \(2\)

The last digit (the 8‑th position) must be even.  
The even digits are \(2,4,6,8\).

---

### 2.  Divisibility by \(11\)

For an 8‑digit number \(d_1d_2\ldots d_8\)

\[
d_1-d_2+d_3-d_4+d_5-d_6+d_7-d_8\equiv 0\pmod{11}.
\]

Let  

\[
S_{\text{odd}} = d_1+d_3+d_5+d_7,\qquad
S_{\text{even}} = d_2+d_4+d_6+d_8 .
\]

Then the condition is \(S_{\text{odd}}-S_{\text{even}}\equiv 0\pmod{11}\).
Since the digits \(1,2,\dots ,8\) sum to \(36\),

\[
S_{\text{odd}}+S_{\text{even}} = 36,
\qquad
S_{\text{odd}}-S_{\text{even}} = 0\Longrightarrow
S_{\text{odd}} = S_{\text{even}} = 18 .
\]

Hence the four digits placed in odd positions must sum to \(18\).

---

### 3.  Choosing the odd–position set

We need the 4‑element subsets of \(\{1,\dots ,8\}\) whose sum is \(18\).

Enumerating them gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\{1,2,7,8\},\; \{1,3,6,8\},\; \{1,4,5,8\},\; \{1,4,6,7\},\\
&\{2,3,5,8\},\; \{2,3,6,7\},\; \{2,4,5,7\},\; \{3,4,5,6\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus there are **8** possible sets for the odd positions.

---

### 4.  Arranging the digits

* For any chosen odd‑position set, its 4 digits can be placed in the odd places
  \((1,3,5,7)\) in \(4! = 24\) ways.

* The complementary even‑position set contains exactly two even and two odd digits
  (each complement also has sum \(18\)).  
  The last digit (position \(8\)) must be even:
  - Choose which of the two even digits goes to position \(8\) – \(2\) ways.
  - Arrange the remaining three digits in positions \(2,4,6\) – \(3! = 6\) ways.

  Hence the even positions can be filled in \(2\cdot 3! = 12\) ways.

Therefore, for each of the 8 admissible odd‑position sets we have  

\[
24 \times 12 = 288
\]

valid permutations.

\[
N = 8 \times 288 = 2304 .
\]

---

### 5.  Required difference

\[
N-2025 = 2304 - 2025 = 279.
\]

\[
\boxed{279}
\]

subject: aime_2025
sample_text:
The two diameters already divide the disk into \(4\) regions.  
Adding a line segment (a chord) to a planar drawing increases the number of
regions by  

\[
1+\text{(number of interior intersections that the new segment makes with
previous segments)} .
\]

Hence, if we let \(I\) be the total number of interior intersection points
among the \(27\) segments, the number of regions is  

\[
R = 1 + 27 + I = 28+I .
\]

So we only have to find the **expected** value of \(I\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Intersections involving the two diameters  

Each random chord meets a given diameter iff its endpoints lie in opposite
half–discs determined by that diameter.  
The two half‑discs are each the union of two quadrants, so a chord’s endpoints
are in opposite halves exactly when the unordered pair of quadrants it uses is
one of the four pairs  

\[
\{1,2\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},
\]

i.e. with probability \(\frac{4}{6}= \frac23\).

Therefore a random chord has expected \(\frac23\) intersections with a given
diameter, and with the two perpendicular diameters its expected number of
intersections is  

\[
2\cdot\frac23 = \frac{4}{3}.
\]

For the \(25\) random chords this contributes  

\[
25\cdot\frac{4}{3}= \frac{100}{3}
\]

intersection points.

The two diameters intersect each other once, so we already have one
intersection.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Intersections among the \(25\) random chords  

Consider two random chords.  
Each chord is chosen by first selecting an unordered pair of different
quadrants (there are \(6\) such pairs, all equally likely) and then picking a
uniform point in each of the two quadrants.

Let the two chords be
\[
\{i,j\},\qquad\{k,\ell\}\qquad(i\neq j,\;k\neq\ell).
\]

*If the two unordered pairs are disjoint* (four distinct quadrants) there are  
three possibilities:

* \(\{1,3\}\) together with \(\{2,4\}\): the chords are opposite
  and **always intersect**;
* the other two possibilities (\(\{1,2\}\) with \(\{3,4\}\) or \(\{2,3\}\) with
  \(\{4,1\}\)): the chords lie in opposite halves and **never intersect**.

Thus for the six ordered possibilities with disjoint pairs the probability of
intersection is \(1\) for two of them and \(0\) for the other four.

*If the two unordered pairs are identical* (the chords use the same two
quadrants), the two points in each quadrant are ordered independently.
The chords intersect exactly when the orders in the two quadrants are opposite,
which happens with probability \(\frac12\).

*If the chords share exactly one quadrant* (three distinct quadrants in total,
say the common quadrant is \(i\)), the two points that lie in the same quadrant
are both inside that quadrant.  The short arc of the circle between them
contains no point of the other chord, so the endpoints cannot be interleaved;
hence such chords **never intersect**.

Collecting the cases:

| # ordered pairs | Intersection probability |
|-----------------|--------------------------|
| identical pairs (6) | \(\frac12\) |
| share one quadrant (24) | \(0\) |
| disjoint opposite pair (2) | \(1\) |
| disjoint adjacent pairs (4) | \(0\) |

Hence the overall probability that two random chords intersect is  

\[
p=\frac{1}{36}\Bigl(6\cdot\frac12+24\cdot0+2\cdot1+4\cdot0\Bigr)
      =\frac{5}{36}.
\]

There are \(\binom{25}{2}=300\) unordered pairs of the random chords, so the
expected number of intersections among them is  

\[
300\cdot p = 300\cdot\frac{5}{36}= \frac{125}{3}=41\frac{2}{3}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Expected total number of intersection points  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[I] &=
\underbrace{1}_{\text{diameters}}+
\underbrace{\frac{100}{3}}_{\text{diameter–chord}}+
\underbrace{\frac{125}{3}}_{\text{chord–chord}}\\[2pt]
&= 1+\frac{100+125}{3}= 1+ \frac{225}{3}=1+75=76 .
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Expected number of regions  

Finally  

\[
\mathbb{E}[R]=28+\mathbb{E}[I]=28+76=104 .
\]

\[
\boxed{104}
\]

subject: aime_2026
sample_text:
The parabola can be written in vertex form  

\[
2y = x^{2}-8x+12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
y=\frac12 (x-4)^{2}-2 .
\]

Its axis of symmetry is the vertical line \(x=4\); the centre of the circle is also on this line:
\(C=(4,39)\).

---

### 1.  Condition for tangency  

Let \((x_0,y_0)\) be a point of the parabola that is tangent to the circle.  
The slope of the parabola at that point is  

\[
y' = \frac{dy}{dx}=x_0-4 .
\]

A radius of a circle is perpendicular to the curve at a point of tangency.  
Thus the vector from the centre to the point, \((x_0-4,\; y_0-39)\), must be parallel to the normal vector \((y',-1)=(x_0-4,-1)\).

Hence  

\[
\frac{x_0-4}{x_0-4}= \frac{y_0-39}{-1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
1=-(y_0-39) .
\]

If \(x_0\neq4\) we obtain  

\[
y_0 = 38 .
\]

If \(x_0 = 4\) then the tangent line is horizontal, the normal is vertical, and any point on the vertical line through the centre works; the only point of the parabola with \(x=4\) is its vertex \((4,-2)\).

---

### 2.  Radii from the two possible tangency points  

**(a) Tangency at the vertex \((4,-2)\).**  

\[
r = \sqrt{(4-4)^2+(-2-39)^2}=| -41| = 41 .
\]

**(b) Tangency where \(y_0=38\).**  

Insert \(y_0=38\) into the parabola equation:

\[
38 = \frac12 (x_0-4)^2 -2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\frac12 (x_0-4)^2 = 40\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
(x_0-4)^2 = 80 .
\]

Thus \(x_0 = 4\pm\sqrt{80}=4\pm4\sqrt{5}\).

The radius is  

\[
r = \sqrt{(x_0-4)^2+(38-39)^2}
    = \sqrt{80+1}= \sqrt{81}=9 .
\]

Both points give the same radius \(r=9\).

---

### 3.  All possible radii  

The circle can be tangent to the parabola for  

\[
r = 9 \qquad\text{or}\qquad r = 41 .
\]

Therefore the sum of all real numbers \(r\) satisfying the condition is  

\[
\boxed{50}.

sample_text:
The operation  

\[
a\circ b=\begin{cases}
a-b,& a\text{ odd and }b\text{ even}\\[2pt]
a+b,&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

is performed from left to right.  
Let the partial result after the first \(i\) terms be \(R_i\) (\(R_1=a_1\)).
If \(R_{i-1}\) is odd and \(a_i\) is even we subtract, otherwise we add:
\[
R_i=\begin{cases}
R_{i-1}-a_i,&R_{i-1}\text{ odd, }a_i\text{ even}\\
R_{i-1}+a_i,&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Parity

Whether we add or subtract does **not** affect parity, because  

\[
\text{odd}-\text{even}\equiv\text{odd} \pmod 2,\qquad 
\text{even}\pm\text{odd/even}\equiv\text{parity}(R_{i-1})\oplus\text{parity}(a_i).
\]

Thus the parity of the running total after \(i\) terms is just the xor of the
parities of the first \(i\) terms.  
Consequently the final result \(R_n\) is even, so the number of odd terms in
the sequence must be even.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Positive and negative contributions  

An odd term is **always added**. An even term is added when the current
running total is even and subtracted when it is odd.  
Hence the even terms are split into two groups:

* **\(E^+\)** – evens that appear while the running total is even,
* **\(E^-\)** – evens that appear while the running total is odd.

If we denote by \(S_{\text{odd}}\) the sum of the odd terms, then

\[
R_n = S_{\text{odd}} + \sum_{e\in E^+} e - \sum_{e\in E^-} e .
\]

Because the total sum of the terms is \(12\),

\[
S_{\text{odd}} + \sum_{e\in E^+} e + \sum_{e\in E^-} e = 12 .
\]

Adding the two equations gives  

\[
2\bigl(S_{\text{odd}} + \sum_{e\in E^+} e\bigr)=12\Longrightarrow 
S_{\text{odd}}+\sum_{e\in E^+}=6 .
\]

Thus we have to split the number \(12\) into  

* a sum \(S_{\text{odd}}\) of an **even number** of odd positive integers,
* a sum \(S_{+}\) of even numbers (the \(E^+\) block),
* a sum \(S_{-}=12-(S_{\text{odd}}+S_{+})\) of even numbers (the \(E^-\) block),

with  

\[
S_{\text{odd}}+S_{+}=6,\qquad S_{-}=6 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Block structure  

Write the sequence as  

\[
E_0^{+}\; O_1\; E_1^{-}\; O_2\; E_2^{+}\; O_3\; E_3^{-}\dots O_k\;E_k^{+},
\]

where the \(O_i\) are the odd terms (there are \(k\) of them, \(k\) even) and
\(E_j^{\pm}\) are (possibly empty) blocks of even numbers.
The signs of the even blocks alternate, starting with a “\(+\)” block.
Hence

* number of “\(+\)” even blocks = \(k+1\),
* number of “\(-\)” even blocks = \(k-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Counting possibilities  

Let  

\[
O=S_{\text{odd}},\qquad P=S_{+},\qquad M=S_{-}=6 .
\]

Because every odd term is at least \(1\),

\[
O\ge k,\qquad O\equiv k\pmod 2 .
\]

The possible values of \(O\) are \(2,4,6\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### **Case \(O=2\)**  

Then \(k=2\) (the only even \(k\le O\)).  
Both odd terms must be \(1\).

* \(P=4\); the three “\(+\)” even blocks must contain a total of \(4\)
  (i.e. two units of “\(2\)”).  
  The number of ways to distribute the two units among the three blocks is
  \(\binom{2+3-1}{3-1}=6\).  Taking into account the internal order of the
  even numbers, this yields \(9\) possibilities.
* The single “\(-\)” block must total \(6\); the number of ordered
  decompositions of \(6\) into even parts is the number of compositions of
  \(3\) into positive integers, \(2^{3-1}=4\).

\[
N_{O=2}=9\cdot4=36 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### **Case \(O=4\)**  

Two possibilities for \(k\).

* **\(k=2\)** : odd terms are \((1,3)\) or \((3,1)\) – \(2\) orders.  
  \(P=2\) (one unit of “\(2\)”), distributed over three “\(+\)” blocks:
  \(\binom{1+3-1}{3-1}=3\) ways, each giving one internal ordering.  
  The single “\(-\)” block contributes \(4\) ways as before.  

  \(N_{k=2}=2\cdot3\cdot4=24\).

* **\(k=4\)** : all four odds are \(1\) (only one order).  
  \(P=2\) again, now distributed over five “\(+\)” blocks:
  \(\binom{1+5-1}{5-1}=5\) ways.  
  The three “\(-\)” blocks must sum to \(6\); by the calculation above they
  give \(25\) possibilities.

  \(N_{k=4}=1\cdot5\cdot25=125\).

\[
N_{O=4}=24+125=149 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### **Case \(O=6\)**  

Possible even \(k\): \(2,4,6\).

* **\(k=2\)** : the two odds can be \((5,1),(1,5),(3,3)\) – \(3\) orders.  
  Here \(P=0\); the single “\(-\)” block contributes \(4\) ways.

  \(N_{k=2}=3\cdot1\cdot4=12\).

* **\(k=4\)** : one odd is \(3\) and the other three are \(1\); the \(3\) can
  occupy any of the four positions – \(4\) orders.  
  Again \(P=0\).  
  The three “\(-\)” blocks give \(25\) possibilities.

  \(N_{k=4}=4\cdot1\cdot25=100\).

* **\(k=6\)** : all six odds are \(1\) (single order).  
  There are five “\(-\)” blocks.  
  Distributing the three units of “\(2\)” among five blocks, the total number
  of possibilities is  

  \[
  \sum_{r=1}^{3}\binom{5}{r}\binom{2}{r-1}2^{3-r}=70 .
  \]

  Hence \(N_{k=6}=1\cdot1\cdot70=70\).

\[
N_{O=6}=12+100+70=182 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Total number of sequences  

\[
\boxed{36+149+182 = 367}
\]

sample_text:
The small sphere of radius \(r=42\) rests on the plane at a point \(P\) of the disk.
If \(P\) is at distance \(d\) from the common centre \(O\) of the disk and the hemisphere,
the centre of the small sphere is at \((d,\, r)\) and its distance from \(O\) is  

\[
OC=\sqrt{d^{2}+r^{2}} .
\]

For the whole sphere to lie inside the hemisphere (radius \(R=200\)),
the farthest point of the small sphere from \(O\) must satisfy  

\[
OC+r\le R .
\]

Thus  

\[
\sqrt{d^{2}+r^{2}}+r\le R\Longrightarrow
\sqrt{d^{2}+r^{2}}\le R-r .
\]

Squaring,

\[
d^{2}+r^{2}\le (R-r)^{2}=R^{2}-2Rr+r^{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
d^{2}\le R^{2}-2Rr .
\]

Plugging \(R=200\) and \(r=42\),

\[
d^{2}\le 200^{2}-2\cdot200\cdot42=40000-16800=23200,
\]
\[
d\le\sqrt{23200}=20\sqrt{58}.
\]

Hence \(\mathcal T\) is a disk of radius \(20\sqrt{58}\).  
The ratio of its area to that of the original disk (radius \(200\)) is  

\[
\frac{\pi(20\sqrt{58})^{2}}{\pi(200)^{2}}
=\frac{400\cdot58}{40000}
=\frac{23200}{40000}
=\frac{29}{50}.
\]

Thus \(\displaystyle\frac{p}{q}= \frac{29}{50}\) with relatively prime \(p,q\), and  

\[
p+q = 29+50 = 79.
\]

\[
\boxed{79}
\]

sample_text:
The centroids and reflections give  

\[
A=(0,0,0),\; B=(6,0,0),\; C=(0,4,0),\qquad 
G=\left(2,\frac43,0\right)
\]

Reflect \(G\) across line \(BC\) to obtain  

\[
D=\left(\frac{42}{13},\frac{124}{39},0\right).
\]

Let the second plane be  

\[
\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z = k ,\qquad \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}=1,
\]

with the spheres touching it on the same side.  
For the sphere centered at \((x_i,y_i,z_i)\) with radius \(r_i\),

\[
k-(\alpha x_i+\beta y_i+\gamma z_i)=r_i .
\]

Using the four given spheres gives  

\[
\begin{cases}
k-\gamma =1,\\
k-6\alpha-2\gamma =2,\\
k-4\beta-3\gamma =3,\\
k-\dfrac{126}{39}\alpha-\dfrac{124}{39}\beta-\gamma r = r .
\end{cases}
\]

From the first three equations,

\[
6\alpha+\gamma=-1,\qquad 2\beta+\gamma=-1,\qquad \beta=3\alpha .
\]

Together with \(\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}=1\) we obtain  

\[
\alpha=-\frac6{23},\qquad \beta=-\frac{18}{23},\qquad 
\gamma=\frac{13}{23},\qquad k=1+\gamma=\frac{36}{23}.
\]

Now solve the fourth equation for \(r\):

\[
r=\frac{\,1+\gamma-\dfrac{126}{39}\alpha-\dfrac{124}{39}\beta\,}{1+\gamma}
   =\frac{\dfrac{1464}{299}}{\dfrac{36}{23}}
   =\frac{122}{39}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle r=\frac{122}{39}}.
\]

The fraction is in lowest terms, so \(m=122,\;n=39\) and  

\[
m+n = 122+39 = \boxed{161}.
\]
