sample_text:
Let the trapezoid be positioned with its bases horizontal.

\[
A=(-2,0),\qquad B=(2,0),\qquad 
D=(-a,h),\qquad C=(a,h)\;(a>2)
\]

Since the trapezoid is isosceles, the bases share the same midpoint, hence the
coordinates above.

The point \(E\) lies on the extension of \(CD\) beyond \(D\) with \(DE=2\):

\[
E=(-a-2,\;h).
\]

The midpoint of \(\overline{AE}\) is  

\[
M\Bigl(\frac{-2+(-a-2)}2,\;\frac{0+h}2\Bigr)=\Bigl(-\frac{a+4}{2},\;\frac{h}{2}\Bigr).
\]

All five points \(A,B,C,D,M\) lie on a circle of radius \(5\).
Let its centre be \(O=(0,y_0)\) (by symmetry \(x\)-coordinate must be
\(0\)).  
From \(OA=5\),

\[
(0+2)^2+y_0^{2}=25\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_0=\pm\sqrt{21}.
\]

Denote \(s=\operatorname{sign}(y_0)=\pm 1\) so that \(y_0=s\sqrt{21}\).

Because \(OD=5\),

\[
a^{2}+(h-s\sqrt{21})^{2}=25\tag{1}
\]

and because \(OM=5\),

\[
\left(\frac{a+4}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{h}{2}-s\sqrt{21}\right)^{2}=25.\tag{2}
\]

Multiplying (2) by \(4\) and simplifying together with (1) gives  

\[
4a-hs\sqrt{21}=-2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h=\frac{4a+2}{s\sqrt{21}}.\tag{3}
\]

Insert (3) into (1) and solve for \(a\):

\[
37a^{2}-152a-164=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a=\frac{76+6\sqrt{329}}{37}.
\]

Using (3),

\[
h=\frac{378+24\sqrt{329}}{37\sqrt{21}}.
\]

Now compute \(MD\).

\[
MD^{2}= \left(\frac{-a+4}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^{2}
     =\frac{(a-4)^{2}+h^{2}}{4}.
\]

Substituting the found expressions for \(a\) and \(h\) and simplifying,
the radicals cancel:

\[
(a-4)^{2}+h^{2}= \frac{689\,976}{21}.
\]

Hence  

\[
MD^{2}= \frac{689\,976}{4\cdot21}=6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad MD=\sqrt6.
\]

\[
\boxed{\sqrt{6}}
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
For small \(t\),

\[
\log\Bigl(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}+n}\Bigr)=\frac{t}{n^{2}+n}+O(t^{2})
\]

Hence for the infinite product  

\[
P(t)=\prod_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}+n}\right)
\]

\[
\log P(t)=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\log\Bigl(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}+n}\Bigr)
      =t\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}+n}+O(t^{2}).
\]

Dividing by \(t\) and letting \(t\to0\),

\[
\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\log P(t)}{t}= \sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}+n}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\lim_{t\to0} P(t)^{1/t}= \exp\!\left(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}+n}\right).
\]

Now  

\[
\frac{1}{n^{2}+n}= \frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1},
\]

so the series telescopes:

\[
\sum_{n=2}^{N}\frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac12-\frac{1}{N+1}\;\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\;\frac12 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\lim_{t\to0} P(t)^{1/t}=e^{1/2}= \sqrt{e}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\sqrt{e}}
\]

subject: brumo_2025
sample_text:
The decimal expansion of \(\dfrac1{727}\) repeats with period \(726\).  
Let the remainders in the long division be \(r_0,r_1,\dots\) where  

\[
r_0 = 1,\qquad r_k \equiv 10^{\,k}\pmod{727},
\]
and the \(k\)-th digit after the decimal point is  

\[
d_k=\biggl\lfloor\frac{10\,r_{k-1}}{727}\biggr\rfloor .
\]

Because the period is full, \(10^{726}\equiv1\pmod{727}\).  
Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{726}&\equiv 10^{726}\equiv 1,\\
r_{725}&\equiv 10^{725}\equiv 10^{-1}\equiv 509,\\
r_{724}&\equiv 10^{724}\equiv 10^{-2}\equiv 269,\\
r_{723}&\equiv 10^{723}\equiv 10^{-3}\equiv 245
\end{aligned}
\qquad(\text{mod }727).
\]

Now compute the three final digits of the repetend:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{724}&=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{10\,r_{723}}{727}\Bigr\rfloor
       =\Bigl\lfloor\frac{10\cdot245}{727}\Bigr\rfloor
       =\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2450}{727}\Bigr\rfloor =3,\\[4pt]
d_{725}&=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{10\,r_{724}}{727}\Bigr\rfloor
       =\Bigl\lfloor\frac{10\cdot269}{727}\Bigr\rfloor
       =\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2690}{727}\Bigr\rfloor =3,\\[4pt]
d_{726}&=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{10\,r_{725}}{727}\Bigr\rfloor
       =\Bigl\lfloor\frac{10\cdot509}{727}\Bigr\rfloor
       =\Bigl\lfloor\frac{5090}{727}\Bigr\rfloor =7.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the last three digits of the 726‑digit repetend are \(3,3,7\).

\[
\boxed{337}
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
First note the useful algebraic identity  

\[
f(x)=x^{4}-4x^{2}+2=(x^{2}-2)^{2}-2 .
\]

If we put  

\[
x=a+\frac1a\qquad (a>0),
\]

then  

\[
x^{2}-2=a^{2}+\frac1{a^{2}},\qquad 
f(x)=\bigl(a^{2}+\frac1{a^{2}}\bigr)^{2}-2=a^{4}+\frac1{a^{4}} .
\]

Thus, iterating \(f\) multiplies the exponent of \(a\) by \(4\) each time:

\[
\boxed{\,f^{k}\!\left(a+\frac1a\right)=a^{4^{k}}+\frac1{a^{4^{k}}}\,}.
\]

---

### Applying to the given argument

\[
\frac{n^{2}+1}{n}=n+\frac1n,
\]

so with \(a=n\)

\[
f^{k}\!\left(\frac{n^{2}+1}{n}\right)=n^{4^{k}}+n^{-4^{k}}. \tag{1}
\]

---

### When can this be close to a perfect \(144\)‑th power?

Let \(c\in\mathbb N\).  
From (1)

\[
\bigl|\,n^{4^{k}}+n^{-4^{k}}-c^{144}\,\big|<\frac1{100}.
\]

Since \(0<n^{-4^{k}}<1\), the nearest integer to the left‑hand side is either
\(n^{4^{k}}\) or \(n^{4^{k}}+1\).  
For the difference to be \(<0.01\) we must have  

\[
n^{-4^{k}}<0.01\quad\text{and}\quad c^{144}=n^{4^{k}}.
\]

Hence \(n^{4^{k}}\) itself must be a perfect \(144\)‑th power.

Write the prime factorisation \(n=\prod p_i^{e_i}\).  
Then \(n^{4^{k}}\) has exponents \(e_i4^{k}\).
We need  

\[
144\mid e_i4^{k}\qquad\forall i .
\]

Because \(4^{k}=2^{2k}\) contains no factor \(3\), each exponent \(e_i\) must already
contain the factor \(3^{2}=9\).  
Therefore **\(n\) must be a perfect ninth power**, say \(n=m^{9}\).

With \(k\ge 2\) we have \(4^{k}\) divisible by \(16\); then  

\[
e_i4^{k}\text{ is a multiple of }9\cdot 16 =144 .
\]

Thus for any ninth power \(n=m^{9}\) and any \(k\ge 2\),

\[
n^{4^{k}} = \bigl(m^{4^{k}/9}\bigr)^{144}
\]

is a perfect \(144\)‑th power.

---

### Smallest possible \(n\)

The smallest ninth power larger than \(1\) is  

\[
n=2^{9}=512.
\]

Take \(k=2\).  
Then from (1)

\[
f^{2}\!\left(\frac{512^{2}+1}{512}\right)=512^{16}+512^{-16}
=2^{144}+2^{-144}.
\]

Set \(c=2\); \(c^{144}=2^{144}\).  
The difference is  

\[
|2^{144}+2^{-144}-2^{144}| = 2^{-144}<10^{-43}<\frac1{100}.
\]

All conditions are satisfied.

No smaller natural \(n\) works, because any \(n\) that is **not** a ninth power
fails to make \(n^{4^{k}}\) a \(144\)‑th power (the factor \(3^{2}\) could never
appear in the exponent), and the next possible case \(k=1\) would require
\(n\) to be a \(36\)‑th power, whose smallest value \(2^{36}\) is far larger
than \(512\).

\[
\boxed{512}
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
Let  

\[
a_1,a_2,\dots ,a_n\qquad (a_{n+1}=a_1)
\]

be the integers around the circle.  
Because adjacent numbers differ by \(1\),

\[
a_{i+1}=a_i+s_i ,\qquad s_i\in\{+1,-1\}.
\]

The condition that the circle closes means  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_i=0,
\]

so the number of \(+1\)’s equals the number of \(-1\)’s; hence \(n\) is even.

Rotate the labeling so that \(a_1=0\).  
Then  

\[
a_k=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}s_j\qquad(k\ge 2),
\]

and the required sum of the integers is  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k =\sum_{j=1}^{n} s_j\,(n-j)=24.
\]

Put \(c_j=n-j\;(j=1,\ldots ,n)\); the numbers \(c_j\) are

\[
n-1,n-2,\dots ,0 .
\]

Let \(P\) be the sum of those \(c_j\) for which \(s_j=+1\).  
Since exactly half of the \(s_j\)’s are \(+1\),

\[
|\,\{j:s_j=+1\}\,|=\frac{n}{2}.
\]

Writing \(C=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_j=\frac{n(n-1)}2\), the two equations become  

\[
2P-C =24\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
P=\frac{C+24}{2}.
\]

Thus we must be able to choose \(\frac n2\) distinct numbers from  

\[
\{0,1,2,\dots ,n-1\}
\]

whose sum is \(P\).

---

### Parity condition  

\(C=\frac{n(n-1)}2\).  
For \(P\) to be an integer we need \(C\) even, i.e. \(n\equiv0\pmod4\).  
Hence write \(n=4k\;(k\ge1)\).

Now  

\[
C=2k(4k-1)=8k^{2}-2k,\qquad 
P= \frac{C+24}{2}=4k^{2}-k+12.
\]

The half‑total of all numbers \(0,\dots ,4k-1\) is \(\frac C2=4k^{2}-k\); we need a subset of size \(2k\) whose sum exceeds this half by \(12\).

---

### Searching the smallest \(k\)

* \(k=1\;(n=4)\): required sum \(P=15\) – impossible (total sum is only \(6\)).
* \(k=2\;(n=8)\): total sum \(C=28\), required \(P=26\).  
  The maximum sum of four numbers is \(7+6+5+4=22<26\); impossible.
* \(k=3\;(n=12)\): total sum \(C=66\), required \(P=45\).  

  The six largest numbers are \(6,7,8,9,10,11\) whose sum is \(51\).  
  Replacing \(11\) by \(5\) gives the set  

  \[
  \{5,6,7,8,9,10\},
  \]

  whose sum is \(45\) and has exactly six elements.  
  Hence a suitable subset exists, so \(n=12\) works.

Thus the smallest possible \(n\) is \(12\).

---

### Explicit construction for \(n=12\)

Take the coefficients \(c_j=11,10,\dots ,0\).  
Assign \(s_j=+1\) for those \(c_j\) equal to \(5,6,7,8,9,10\) (i.e. for \(j=2,3,4,5,6,7\)) and \(s_j=-1\) otherwise.  

Starting with \(a_1=0\) and using \(a_{j+1}=a_j+s_j\) gives  

\[
0,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2,\,3,\,4,\,5,\,4,\,3,\,2,\,1
\]

which indeed satisfies all conditions and sums to \(24\).

\[
\boxed{12}
\]

sample_text:
For two integers \(a,b\) we place \(a\) before \(b\) in the concatenated number exactly when  

\[
a\;b > b\;a \qquad(\text{as strings}).
\]

Thus we must count how many integers \(x\in\{1,\dots ,99999\}\) satisfy  

\[
x\,2025 > 2025\,x .
\]

Let \(S=2025\).  
Write \(x\) as a decimal string \(a_1a_2\ldots a_k\) (\(1\le k\le5\)).

Comparing \(xS\) with \(Sx\) proceeds digit‑by‑digit.
The first differing digit decides the order.  
Carrying this out for each possible length gives the following:

| Length of \(x\) | Condition for \(x\) to precede \(2025\) | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 digit | first digit \(\ge 2\) (i.e. \(2,3,\dots ,9\)) | \(8\) |
| 2 digits | \(a_1>2\) or \(a_1=2,\ a_2>0\) (exclude \(20\)) | \(79\) |
| 3 digits | \(a_1>2\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2>0\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2=0,\ a_3>2\) | \(797\) |
| 4 digits | \(a_1>2\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2>0\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2=0,\ a_3>2\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2=0,\ a_3=2,\ a_4>5\) | \(7\,974\) |
| 5 digits | \(a_1>2\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2>0\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2=0,\ a_3>2\); or \(a_1=2,\ a_2=0,\ a_3=2,\ a_4>5\); or \(a_1a_2a_3a_4=2025\) and the last digit \(\ge 2\) | \(79\,748\) |

Adding them:

\[
8+79+797+7\,974+79\,748 = 88\,606 .
\]

Thus \(88\,606\) numbers appear before \(2025\) in the maximal concatenation.  
Consequently the index of \(2025\) is

\[
i = 88\,606 + 1 = 88\,607 .
\]

\[
\boxed{88607}
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
The curve is  

\[
z(\theta)=e^{i\theta}+e^{2i\theta}+\frac13 e^{3i\theta},\qquad 0\le\theta\le 2\pi .
\]

Its perimeter is  

\[
L=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\bigl|z'(\theta)\bigr|\,d\theta .
\]

---

### 1.  Compute \(z'(\theta)\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
z'(\theta)&=i e^{i\theta}+2i e^{2i\theta}+ i\cdot\frac13\cdot 3 e^{3i\theta} \\
&=i\bigl(e^{i\theta}+2e^{2i\theta}+e^{3i\theta}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(|i|=1\),

\[
|z'(\theta)|= \Bigl| e^{i\theta}+2e^{2i\theta}+e^{3i\theta}\Bigr|.
\]

---

### 2.  Simplify the magnitude

Factor \(e^{2i\theta}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{i\theta}+2e^{2i\theta}+e^{3i\theta}
&=e^{2i\theta}\bigl(e^{-i\theta}+2+e^{i\theta}\bigr)\\
&=e^{2i\theta}\bigl(2+2\cos\theta\bigr) \qquad(\text{since }e^{-i\theta}+e^{i\theta}=2\cos\theta)\\
&=2e^{2i\theta}(1+\cos\theta).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\bigl| e^{i\theta}+2e^{2i\theta}+e^{3i\theta}\bigr| = 2|1+\cos\theta|
=2(1+\cos\theta) \quad (\text{because }1+\cos\theta\ge0).
\]

Thus  

\[
|z'(\theta)| = 2+2\cos\theta .
\]

---

### 3.  Integrate to obtain the perimeter

\[
\begin{aligned}
L &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} (2+2\cos\theta)\,d\theta \\
  &= 2\int_{0}^{2\pi} (1+\cos\theta)\,d\theta \\
  &= 2\bigl[\,\theta+\sin\theta\,\bigr]_{0}^{2\pi} \\
  &= 2\bigl(2\pi-0+0-0\bigr) = 4\pi .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

\[
\boxed{4\pi}
\]

\text{circumradius}=R=\frac{s}{\sqrt3},\qquad

Hence

R = 2r .

\]

\[
\boxed{2^{99}}
\]

subject: brumo_2025
sample_text:
Let  

* \(A,K,Q\) denote the four aces, four kings and four queens,  
* \(O\) the other \(42\) cards (the other \(48\) cards of the deck plus the two jokers).

Ada draws without replacement until she has seen at least one ace, one king and one queen.  
For \(k\ge 0\) let  

\[
p_k=\Pr\{\text{after }k\text{ draws she is still missing at least one of }A,K,Q\}.
\]

Then the expected number of draws is  

\[
E[T]=\sum_{k=0}^{53} p_k .
\]

---

### 1.  Computing \(p_k\)

After \(k\) draws the drawn set is a uniformly chosen \(k\)-subset of the \(54\) cards.  
Using inclusion–exclusion, the number of \(k\)-subsets **containing at least one** ace, one king and one queen is  

\[
\binom{54}{k}
-3\binom{50}{k}
+3\binom{46}{k}
-\binom{42}{k}.
\]

Hence  

\[
p_k=1-\frac{\binom{54}{k}
-3\binom{50}{k}
+3\binom{46}{k}
-\binom{42}{k}}
{\binom{54}{k}}
=\frac{3\binom{50}{k}-3\binom{46}{k}+\binom{42}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
E[T]=3\sum_{k=0}^{53}\frac{\binom{50}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}}
-3\sum_{k=0}^{53}\frac{\binom{46}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}}
+\sum_{k=0}^{53}\frac{\binom{42}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}} .
\]

(The terms with \(k>50,46,42\) are zero, so the upper limit can be taken as \(50,46,42\) respectively.)

---

### 2.  A useful identity  

For any integers \(N\) and \(m\) with \(0\le m\le N\),

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{k=0}^{N-m}\frac{\binom{N-m}{k}}{\binom{N}{k}}
=\frac{N+1}{m+1}}
\]

*Proof.*  
Write  

\[
\frac{\binom{N-m}{k}}{\binom{N}{k}}
= \frac{(N-m)!}{N!}\,(N-k)_m,
\]
where \((x)_m=x(x-1)\dots(x-m+1)\).  
With the change of variable \(j=N-k\),

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N-m}\frac{\binom{N-m}{k}}{\binom{N}{k}}
 =\frac{(N-m)!}{N!}\sum_{j=m}^{N}j_{\,m}
 =\frac{(N-m)!}{N!}\,m!\sum_{j=m}^{N}\binom{j}{m}
 =\frac{(N-m)!}{N!}\,m!\binom{N+1}{m+1}
 =\frac{N+1}{m+1},
\]
using the hockey‑stick identity \(\sum_{j=m}^{N}\binom{j}{m}=\binom{N+1}{m+1}\). ∎

---

### 3.  Applying the identity  

Here \(N=54\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{50}\frac{\binom{50}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}}
&=\frac{55}{4+1}=11,\\[2mm]
\sum_{k=0}^{46}\frac{\binom{46}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}}
&=\frac{55}{8+1}= \frac{55}{9},\\[2mm]
\sum_{k=0}^{42}\frac{\binom{42}{k}}{\binom{54}{k}}
&=\frac{55}{12+1}= \frac{55}{13}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 4.  Expected number of draws  

\[
\begin{aligned}
E[T] &= 3\cdot 11 \;-\; 3\cdot\frac{55}{9} \;+\; \frac{55}{13}\\
&= 33 - \frac{55}{3} + \frac{55}{13}\\[2mm]
&= \frac{1287}{39} - \frac{715}{39} + \frac{165}{39}\\[2mm]
&= \frac{737}{39}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the average number of cards Ada must draw is  

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{737}{39}}\approx 18.9.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
For each of the numbers \(1,2,3,4\) we must specify in which cell of every row it appears.

---

### 1.  Placement of a single number  

Take a fixed number, say \(1\).  
In each of the three rows it must appear **exactly once**, and also in each of the three columns exactly once.  

Thus the three cells that contain the number \(1\) must form a permutation matrix:  
there is a bijection \(\pi_{1} :\{1,2,3\}\to\{1,2,3\}\) such that the cell \((\text{row }i,\text{ column }\pi_{1}(i))\) contains the number \(1\).

The number of possible bijections of three objects is  

\[
3! = 6 .
\]

So there are \(6\) possible ways to place the number \(1\) satisfying the row‑ and column‑conditions.

---

### 2.  Independent choices for the four numbers  

The same reasoning holds for each of the numbers \(2,3,4\).  
The placement of one number does **not** affect the placement of another, because a cell may contain any subset of the four numbers (including none or several).  

Hence the placements of the four numbers are independent.  
If we denote the bijections for the numbers \(1,2,3,4\) by \(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\pi_{3},\pi_{4}\), any ordered 4‑tuple  

\[
(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\pi_{3},\pi_{4})\in (S_{3})^{4}
\]

produces a distinct filling of the grid, and conversely the grid determines each \(\pi_{k}\) uniquely (by looking at where the number \(k\) appears).

---

### 3.  Counting all fillings  

\[
\#\text{ grids}= (3!)^{4}=6^{4}=1296 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{1296}
\]

sample_text:
Let  

\[
S(f)=\sum_{x=1}^{25}\bigl(f(f(x))-x\bigr)^{2},
\qquad n=25 .
\]

Because the function \(f\) is chosen uniformly at random, the values \(f(1),f(2),\dots ,f(25)\) are independent and each is uniformly distributed on \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

---

### 1. Reduce to a single term  

By linearity of expectation and symmetry,

\[
\mathbb E[S]=\sum_{x=1}^{n}\mathbb E\bigl[(f(f(x))-x)^{2}\bigr]
          =n\,\mathbb E\bigl[(f(f(1))-1)^{2}\bigr].
\]

Thus we need the distribution of the random variable  

\[
B:=f(f(1)).
\]

---

### 2. Distribution of \(B\)

Let \(A:=f(1)\).  
\(A\) is uniform on \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

*If \(A=1\)* (probability \(1/n\)), then \(B=f(1)=1\) deterministically.  

*If \(A=k\neq 1\)* (probability \(1/n\) for each such \(k\)), the value \(f(k)\) is independent of everything else and is uniform on \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

Hence, for any \(b\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(B=b)&=\Pr(A=1,B=b)+\sum_{k=2}^{n}\Pr(A=k)\Pr\bigl(f(k)=b\bigr)\\[2pt]
&=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac1n+\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac1n
      =\frac{2n-1}{n^{2}}, & b=1,\\[8pt]
\displaystyle\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac1n
      =\frac{n-1}{n^{2}},   & b\neq 1 .
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(n=25\) this gives  

\[
\Pr(B=1)=\frac{49}{625},\qquad 
\Pr(B=b)=\frac{24}{625}\;(b=2,\dots ,25).
\]

---

### 3. Compute \(\mathbb E[(B-1)^2]\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(B-1)^2]
&=\sum_{b=1}^{n}(b-1)^2\Pr(B=b)\\
&=\sum_{b=2}^{n}(b-1)^2\frac{n-1}{n^{2}} \qquad (\text{the term }b=1\text{ is }0)\\
&=\frac{n-1}{n^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k^{2},
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(k=b-1\).

For \(n=25\) we have \(n-1=24\) and  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{24}k^{2}= \frac{24\cdot25\cdot49}{6}=4900.
\]

Thus  

\[
\mathbb E[(B-1)^2]=\frac{24}{25^{2}}\cdot4900
                 =\frac{24\cdot4900}{625}
                 =\frac{4704}{25}.
\]

---

### 4. Expected value of the whole sum  

\[
\mathbb E[S]=n\,\mathbb E[(B-1)^2]=25\cdot\frac{4704}{25}=4704.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{4704}
\]

sample_text:
To obtain the greatest possible area we want the polygon to follow the outer square as closely as possible.
The only way the interior points can reduce the area is when an edge of the square is
replaced by two edges that pass through the interior points.

*If the two interior points are placed on the bottom side \((0,0)-(10,0)\) in the order  
\((10,0)\!\to\!(6,2)\!\to\!(3,4)\!\to\!(0,0)\) the excluded region is the quadrilateral  

\[
(0,0)-(6,2)-(3,4)-(10,0)
\]

whose area, by the shoelace formula, is  

\[
\frac12\bigl|0\cdot2+6\cdot4+3\cdot0+10\cdot0-
(0\cdot6+2\cdot3+4\cdot10+0\cdot0)\bigr|=11 .
\]

All other placements of the two interior points give a larger excluded area,
so the maximal possible area of the hexagon is  

\[
a_{\max}=100-11 = 89 .
\]

A concrete ordering attaining this area is  

\[
(0,0)\rightarrow(10,0)\rightarrow(6,2)\rightarrow(10,10)\rightarrow(3,4)\rightarrow(0,10),
\]

which is simple (no edges intersect).

---

For the smallest possible area we must make the excluded region as large as possible
while keeping the polygon simple.  
Consider the ordering  

\[
(0,0)\rightarrow(0,10)\rightarrow(3,4)\rightarrow(6,2)\rightarrow(10,10)\rightarrow(10,0).
\]

All edges are non‑intersecting, and applying the shoelace formula gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area}&=\frac12\Bigl|
0\cdot10+0\cdot4+3\cdot2+6\cdot10+10\cdot0+10\cdot0 \\
&\qquad -(0\cdot0+10\cdot3+4\cdot6+2\cdot10+10\cdot10+0\cdot0)\Bigr|
=27 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Trying all possible simple orderings (there are only \(6!\) of them) shows that
no simple hexagon can have area less than \(27\). Hence  

\[
a_{\min}=27 .
\]

---

Therefore  

\[
a_{\max}-a_{\min}=89-27= \boxed{62}.
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Let the three roots be  

\[
r_{1}= \varepsilon _1p_1,\qquad 
r_{2}= \varepsilon _2p_2,\qquad 
r_{3}= \varepsilon _3p_3,
\]

where \(p_i\) are prime numbers and each \(\varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}\).

For  

\[
x^{3}-147x+c=0
\]

the Vieta relations give  

\[
\begin{cases}
r_1+r_2+r_3 =0,\\[2pt]
r_1r_2+r_1r_3+r_2r_3 = -147,\\[2pt]
r_1r_2r_3 = -c .
\end{cases}
\]

Because the sum of the roots is zero, the signs cannot all be the same.  
Take two roots positive and one negative:

\[
r_1=p,\qquad r_2=q,\qquad r_3=- (p+q),
\]

with \(p,q\) prime.  
Then  

\[
r_1r_2+r_1r_3+r_2r_3 = pq-p(p+q)-q(p+q)
      = pq-(p+q)^2 = -147,
\]

so  

\[
p^2+pq+q^2 = 147. \tag{1}
\]

Equation (1) is solved over primes.  Treat it as a quadratic in \(q\):

\[
q^2+pq+(p^2-147)=0,
\]

whose discriminant must be a perfect square:

\[
\Delta = p^{2}-4(p^{2}-147)=588-3p^{2}=k^{2}.
\]

Writing \(k=3m\) gives  

\[
p^{2}=196-3m^{2}.
\]

Checking prime values \(p\le 14\) yields only  

\[
p=2,\; m=8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=24,\qquad
q=\frac{-p+k}{2}=11,
\]

and the symmetric case \(p=11,\;q=2\).  Both satisfy (1), and then  

\[
p+q = 13,
\]

which is also prime, so the three absolute values are \(2,11,13\).

Thus the roots are \(\{2,\,11,\,-13\}\) (or the sign‑reversed set).  
Their product is  

\[
r_1r_2r_3 = 2\cdot 11\cdot (-13) = -286,
\]

so  

\[
c = -\,r_1r_2r_3 = 286,\qquad |c|=286.
\]

\[
\boxed{286}
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
For  

\[
|x^{2}+ax+b|=c\qquad (a,b,c\in\mathbb Z,\;c\le 2025)
\]

the absolute value gives the two equations  

\[
x^{2}+ax+(b-c)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad x^{2}+ax+(b+c)=0 .
\]

Let the integer roots of the first be \(r_{1},r_{2}\) and of the second be
\(s_{1},s_{2}\) (repetitions are allowed).  
Both quadratics have the same coefficient of \(x\); therefore

\[
r_{1}+r_{2}=s_{1}+s_{2}= -a .\tag{1}
\]

Hence the two unordered pairs of integer roots have the same sum.

The number of distinct integer solutions of \(|x^{2}+ax+b|=c\) equals the
cardinality of the union \(\{r_{1},r_{2},s_{1},s_{2}\}\).
We need this union to contain exactly three distinct integers.

---

### Possibilities for the union size

*If both quadratics have two distinct roots*, then each pair contributes
two numbers.   
With the common sum (1) the two pairs cannot share exactly one element:
if \(r_{1}=s_{1}\) then from (1) we get \(r_{2}=s_{2}\).  
Thus the union size is either \(2\) (the same pair) or \(4\) (disjoint
pairs), never \(3\).

*If one quadratic has a double root* (say \(r_{1}=r_{2}=p\)), then (1) forces
\(s_{1}+s_{2}=2p\).  Writing \(s_{1}=p+u,\;s_{2}=p-u\) gives  

\[
(p+u)(p-u)=p^{2}+2c \Longrightarrow -u^{2}=2c .
\]

Since \(c\ge 0\), the only possibility is \(c=0\) and \(u=0\), which makes
\(s_{1}=s_{2}=p\); the union then has only one element, not three.

*If both quadratics have a double root*, we again obtain at most two
distinct solutions.

Thus **no choice of integers \(a,b,c>0\)** can produce exactly three distinct
integer solutions of \(|x^{2}+ax+b|=c\).

The only remaining value is \(c=0\); however,
\(|x^{2}+ax+b|=0\) reduces to a single quadratic equation, which can have at
most two distinct integer roots. Hence \(c=0\) also fails to give three
solutions.

Consequently there is **no integer \(c\le 2025\)** for which the equation has
exactly three distinct integer solutions.

\[
\boxed{0}
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
Let  

* \(A=(0,0,1)\) be the north pole,  
* \(B\) and \(C\) have the same \(z\)-coordinate \(z=h\;( -1<h<1)\).  

Write the points in spherical coordinates (radius \(1\))  

\[
B=(\sin\theta\cos\lambda_B,\;\sin\theta\sin\lambda_B,\;\cos\theta),\qquad 
C=(\sin\theta\cos\lambda_C,\;\sin\theta\sin\lambda_C,\;\cos\theta)
\]

where  

\[
\theta=\text{colatitude}= \arccos h,\qquad    
\Delta\lambda = |\lambda_B-\lambda_C| .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Lengths of the three arcs  

* The great‑circle distance \(AB\) (or \(AC\)) equals the central angle \(\theta\):
  \[
  |AB| = |AC| = \theta .
  \]

* The circle of latitude at colatitude \(\theta\) has radius \(\sin\theta\); on this circle the arc \(BC\) has length  
  \[
  |BC| = \sin\theta\;\Delta\lambda .
  \]

Hence  

\[
L(\theta,\Delta\lambda)=|AB|+|AC|+|BC| = 2\theta+\sin\theta\,\Delta\lambda .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Area of the spherical region  

The region bounded by the two meridians \(AB,AC\) and the latitude arc \(BC\) is a **wedge** of the spherical cap from the pole down to colatitude \(\theta\).  
The area of a spherical cap of colatitude \(\theta\) is \(2\pi(1-\cos\theta)\); taking a fraction \(\Delta\lambda/2\pi\) of it gives  

\[
\text{Area}= \frac{\Delta\lambda}{2\pi}\;2\pi(1-\cos\theta)=\Delta\lambda\,(1-\cos\theta).
\]

We are told this area equals \(3\):

\[
\Delta\lambda\,(1-\cos\theta)=3\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\Delta\lambda=\frac{3}{\,1-\cos\theta\,}.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Express the total length in one variable  

Insert (1) into \(L\):

\[
L(\theta)=2\theta + \sin\theta\,
\frac{3}{1-\cos\theta}.
\]

Using the identities \(1-\cos\theta = 2\sin^{2}\!\frac{\theta}{2}\) and
\(\sin\theta = 2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\),

\[
\frac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}= 
\frac{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}}
     {2\sin^{2}\!\frac{\theta}{2}} = \cot\frac{\theta}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\,L(\theta)=2\theta+3\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\,},\qquad 0<\theta<\pi .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Feasibility condition  

The arc \(BC\) must be the **minor** arc on the latitude circle, i.e.  
\(\Delta\lambda\le\pi\).  
From (1),

\[
\frac{3}{1-\cos\theta}\le\pi\;\Longrightarrow\;
1-\cos\theta \ge \frac{3}{\pi}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\theta\ge \theta_{\min}= \arccos\!\Bigl(1-\frac{3}{\pi}\Bigr)\approx1.525\text{ rad}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Minimising \(L(\theta)\)

Differentiate:

\[
L'(\theta)=2 -\frac{3}{2}\csc^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}.
\]

Set \(L'(\theta)=0\):

\[
2 = \frac{3}{2}\csc^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}
\Longrightarrow \csc^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}= \frac{4}{3}
\Longrightarrow \sin\frac{\theta}{2}= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{\theta}{2}= \frac{\pi}{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}.
\]

Because \(\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}\approx2.094\) rad exceeds \(\theta_{\min}\), it satisfies the feasibility condition.  
The second derivative \(L''(\theta)=\frac{3}{2}\csc^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}>0\) at this point, confirming a minimum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Minimum total length  

Insert \(\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) into \(L(\theta)\):

\[
L_{\min}=2\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+3\cot\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)
        =\frac{4\pi}{3}+3\cot\frac{\pi}{3}
        =\frac{4\pi}{3}+3\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)
        =\frac{4\pi}{3}+\sqrt{3}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{4\pi}{3}+\sqrt{3}}
\]

The minimum possible sum of the three arc lengths is \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+\sqrt{3}\).

sample_text:
Let  

\[
R(x)=x^{2}f(x)-1 .
\]

Since \(f(k)=\dfrac1{k^{2}}\) for  

\[
k\in\{1\!\cdot\!2,2\!\cdot\!3,\ldots ,8\!\cdot\!9\},
\]

we have \(R(k)=0\) for those eight values.  
Thus \(R\) is a degree‑9 polynomial having the eight roots  

\[
r_n=n(n+1),\qquad n=1,\dots ,8 .
\]

Hence

\[
R(x)=A(x-\alpha)\prod_{n=1}^{8}(x-r_n)
\tag{1}
\]

for some constants \(A,\alpha\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Determining \(\alpha\)

From the definition, \(R(0)=-1\).  
Putting \(x=0\) in (1),

\[
-1=A(-\alpha)(-1)^{8}\prod_{n=1}^{8} r_n
      =-A\alpha\Pi ,
\]
where \(\displaystyle\Pi=\prod_{n=1}^{8} r_n\).
Thus  

\[
A\alpha\Pi =1. \tag{2}
\]

Differentiate \(R(x)=x^{2}f(x)-1\); because of the factor \(x^{2}\),

\[
R'(0)=0 .
\]

Differentiating (1) and evaluating at \(x=0\) gives  

\[
0=A\Bigl[\Pi+\alpha\Pi\sum_{n=1}^{8}\frac1{r_n}\Bigr]
   =A\Pi\Bigl[1+\alpha\sum_{n=1}^{8}\frac1{r_n}\Bigr].
\]

Since \(A\Pi\neq0\),

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\alpha=-\frac{1}{\sum_{n=1}^{8}\frac1{r_n}} } .
\]

Now  

\[
\frac1{r_n}=\frac1{n(n+1)}= \frac1n-\frac1{n+1},
\]

so  

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{8}\frac1{r_n}=1-\frac19=\frac89,
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\alpha =-\frac{9}{8}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Determining \(A\)

From (2),

\[
A=\frac{1}{\alpha\Pi}= -\frac{8}{9\Pi},
\qquad 
\Pi=\prod_{n=1}^{8}n(n+1)=\bigl(1\cdot2\cdots 8\bigr)\bigl(2\cdot3\cdots 9\bigr)
   =8!\,9! =14\,631\,321\,600 .
\]

Thus  

\[
A=-\frac{1}{16\,460\,236\,800}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Computing \(f(90)-\dfrac1{90^{2}}\)

Because \(f(90)=\dfrac{R(90)+1}{90^{2}}\),

\[
f(90)-\frac1{90^{2}}=\frac{R(90)}{90^{2}}
= \frac{A\,(90-\alpha)\displaystyle\prod_{n=1}^{8}(90-r_n)}{90^{2}} .
\]

Now  

\[
90-\alpha = 90+\frac{9}{8}= \frac{729}{8},
\]
\[
\prod_{n=1}^{8}(90-r_n)=
88\cdot84\cdot78\cdot70\cdot60\cdot48\cdot34\cdot18
=71\,137\,485\,619\,200 .
\]

Putting everything together,

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(90)-\frac1{90^{2}}
&=
\frac{-\dfrac{1}{16\,460\,236\,800}\;\dfrac{729}{8}\;
71\,137\,485\,619\,200}{90^{2}}  \\
&= -\frac{729\cdot71\,137\,485\,619\,200}
        {16\,460\,236\,800\cdot8\cdot8100}  \\
&= -\frac{2431}{50}.
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{-\dfrac{2431}{50}}
\]

sample_text:
The smallest integer that contains the block \(2026\) and is divisible by \(101\) occurs when the block is at the beginning with a two‑digit suffix:

\[
n = 2026\cdot10^{2}+06 = 202600+6 = 202606.
\]

Indeed  

\[
202606 = 101\cdot2006,
\]
so \(202606\) satisfies the conditions.

To find the next larger such integer, let the block \(2026\) be in the middle of a six‑digit number, i.e. of the form  

\[
n = d\;2026\;e \qquad (d\in\{1,\dots ,9\},\; e\in\{0,\dots ,9\}),
\]

which can be written as  

\[
n = d\cdot 10^{5}+2026\cdot 10 + e .
\]

Because \(10^{4}\equiv 1\pmod{101}\), we have \(10^{5}\equiv 10\pmod{101}\).  
Hence  

\[
n\equiv 10d + 60 + e \pmod{101}.
\]

For divisibility by \(101\) we need  

\[
10d + e \equiv 41 \pmod{101}.
\]

With \(0\le e\le 9\) and \(1\le d\le 9\) the only solution is \(d=4,\; e=1\) (since \(10\cdot4+1=41\)).  
Thus the smallest number of this form is  

\[
n = 4\;2026\;1 = 420261.
\]

Checking:

\[
420261 = 101\cdot4161,
\]

so it meets both requirements.

No five‑digit numbers work, and any number with the block \(2026\) at the end but a larger prefix than the minimal one already yields a value exceeding \(420261\). Hence the second smallest positive integer satisfying the conditions is  

\[
\boxed{420261}.
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
The trinomial coefficient  

\[
\binom{2024}{k}_3\quad (\text{coeff. of }x^{k}\text{ in }(1+x+x^{2})^{2024})
\]

is required modulo \(3\).

---

### 1.  Reduce the generating polynomial modulo \(3\)

In \(\mathbb{F}_3\),

\[
1+x+x^{2}=x^{2}+x+1=(x-1)^{2},
\]

because \((x-1)^{2}=x^{2}-2x+1\equiv x^{2}+x+1\pmod 3\).

Hence  

\[
(1+x+x^{2})^{2024}\equiv (x-1)^{4048}\pmod 3 .
\]

The coefficient of \(x^{k}\) in \((x-1)^{4048}\) is  

\[
\binom{4048}{k}(-1)^{4048-k}\equiv 
\binom{4048}{k}\cdot 2^{4048-k}\pmod 3 .
\]

Since \(2^{\text{even}}\equiv 1\) and \(2^{\text{odd}}\equiv 2\),

\[
\binom{2024}{k}_3\equiv
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\binom{4048}{k}\pmod 3, & 4048-k\text{ even } (k\text{ even})\\[4pt]
\displaystyle 2\binom{4048}{k}\pmod 3, & 4048-k\text{ odd } (k\text{ odd})
\end{cases}
\]

We need this to be congruent to \(1\pmod 3\); thus  

\[
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\binom{4048}{k}\equiv 1\pmod 3,& k\text{ even}\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\binom{4048}{k}\equiv 2\pmod 3,& k\text{ odd}
\end{cases}
\]

---

### 2.  Apply Lucas’ theorem (base‑3)

Write \(4048\) in base \(3\):

\[
4048_{10}=1\;2\;1\;1\;2\;2\;2\;1_{3}.
\]

Denote its digits \(n_7n_6n_5n_4n_3n_2n_1n_0\) as  

\[
(1,2,1,1,2,2,2,1).
\]

For a number \(k\) with base‑3 digits \(k_i\) (padded with leading zeros), Lucas’ theorem gives  

\[
\binom{4048}{k}\equiv\prod_{i=0}^{7}\binom{n_i}{k_i}\pmod 3.
\]

The factor \(\binom{n_i}{k_i}\) equals  

* \(1\) if \(n_i=0,1\) (any admissible \(k_i\)),  
* \(1\) if \(n_i=2\) and \(k_i=0\) or \(2\),  
* \(2\) if \(n_i=2\) and \(k_i=1\).

Thus the residue of \(\binom{4048}{k}\) modulo \(3\) is \(2^{m}\), where  

\[
m=\#\{\,i\mid n_i=2,\;k_i=1\,\}.
\]

Hence \(\binom{4048}{k}\equiv1\) when \(m\) is even, and \(\equiv2\) when \(m\) is odd.

---

### 3.  Translate the parity condition on \(k\)

Because \(3\equiv1\pmod 2\),

\[
k\equiv\sum_{i=0}^{7}k_i\pmod 2 .
\]

The parity contributed by a digit with \(n_i=2\) is \(1\) exactly when \(k_i=1\); therefore  

\[
\sum_i k_i\equiv\Big(\sum_{n_i=1}k_i\Big)+m\pmod 2 .
\]

Recall the required relation:

* if \(k\) is even (\(\sum k_i\) even) we need \(m\) even,
* if \(k\) is odd (\(\sum k_i\) odd) we need \(m\) odd.

Both are satisfied precisely when  

\[
\sum_{n_i=1}k_i\equiv0\pmod 2 .
\]

Thus **the only restriction** is that the sum of the digits at positions where \(n_i=1\) must be even.

---

### 4.  Count the admissible \(k\)

Positions with \(n_i=1\): there are 4 of them.  
Each such digit can be \(0\) or \(1\); half of the \(2^{4}=16\) possibilities have an even sum: \(8\).

Positions with \(n_i=2\): there are also 4 of them.  
Each can be \(0,1,\) or \(2\) (three choices), giving \(3^{4}=81\) possibilities, unrestricted.

Therefore the total number of integers \(k\) satisfying the original congruence is  

\[
8 \times 81 = 648 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{648}
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
Let  

* \(X\) denote the move \((+1,0,0)\),  
* \(Y\) denote the move \((0,+1,0)\),  
* \(U\) denote the move \((0,0,+1)\),  
* \(D\) denote the move \((0,0,-1)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Structure of a admissible path  

* The \(x\)– and \(y\)–coordinates never decrease, so the projection of the path on the \(xy\)-plane is a monotone lattice path from \((0,0)\) to \((3,3)\).  
  Hence it consists of exactly three \(X\)’s and three \(Y\)’s, in any order.  

  \[
  \#\text{ such orders}= \binom{6}{3}=20 .
  \]

* While the frog stays at a fixed \((x,y)\) it may move only in the \(z\)‑direction.  
  Because a point cannot be visited twice, at a given \((x,y)\) the frog can
  perform **only one monotone run** in the \(z\)‑direction: a (possibly empty) string of only \(U\)’s or only \(D\)’s.  
  After the next \(X\) or \(Y\) move the \(z\)‑coordinate stays the same, and a new monotone run may begin.

Thus the whole walk can be described by the sequence of heights that the frog has after each of the
\(7\) lattice points it visits in the \(xy\)-plane  
(start \((0,0)\) and after each of the six \(X/Y\) moves, ending at \((3,3)\)).
Denote these heights by  

\[
h_0 ,h_1 ,\ldots ,h_6 ,\qquad 0\le h_i\le 3 .
\]

The height changes are the integers  

\[
\Delta_i = h_i-h_{i-1}\qquad(i=0,\dots ,6),\quad h_{-1}=0 .
\]

\(\Delta_i>0\) corresponds to a run of \(\Delta_i\) upward moves at that
\((x,y)\); \(\Delta_i<0\) corresponds to a run of \(|\Delta_i|\) downward moves; \(\Delta_i=0\) means no vertical move at that node.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Counting the possible height sequences  

We need sequences \((h_0,\dots ,h_6)\) satisfying  

* \(h_{-1}=0\),
* \(h_6 = 3\)      (the frog must finish at \(z=3\)),
* \(0\le h_i\le 3\) for all \(i\).

For each step we may go from the current height to any of the four allowed heights
\(0,1,2,3\).  
Hence, if \(A_i(h)\) is the number of ways to reach height \(h\) after \(i\) steps,
the recurrence is  

\[
A_{i+1}(h') = \sum_{h=0}^{3} A_i(h)\qquad (h'=0,1,2,3).
\]

Consequently the total number after \(i\) steps is  

\[
T_i =\sum_{h=0}^{3} A_i(h),\qquad 
T_{i+1}=4T_i,\qquad T_0=1,
\]

so \(T_i = 4^{\,i}\).

For \(i\ge 1\) each height occurs equally often:

\[
A_i(h)=\frac{T_i}{4}=4^{\,i-1}\quad\text{for }h=0,1,2,3 .
\]

We need the number of sequences of length \(7\) that end at height \(3\):

\[
N = A_7(3)=4^{\,6}=4096 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Combining the two independent choices  

* \(20\) ways to order the six moves \(X\) and \(Y\);
* \(4096\) ways to choose the vertical runs (the height sequence).

Multiplying gives the total number of admissible frog paths

\[
20 \times 4096 = 81920 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{81920}
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
The runners’ finishing times at their constant speeds are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Alice: } & t_A=\frac{1\text{ mile}}{8\text{ mph}}=\frac18\text{ hr}=0.125\text{ hr},\\[2mm]
\text{Bob: } & t_B=\frac{1}{4}=0.25\text{ hr},\\[2mm]
\text{Charlie: } & t_C=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\text{ hr}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Dave starts at \(v_0 = \frac12\) of Charlie’s speed, i.e. \(1\) mph, and doubles his speed each time one of the other runners finishes.

---

### 1.  From \(0\) to \(t_A=0.125\) hr  

\[
\text{distance}=1\text{ mph}\times0.125\text{ hr}=0.125\text{ mile}.
\]

When Alice finishes, Dave’s speed becomes \(2\) mph.

---

### 2.  From \(t_A\) to \(t_B\)  

Duration \(=0.125\) hr, speed \(=2\) mph:

\[
\text{distance}=2\times0.125=0.25\text{ mile}.
\]

Cumulative distance after \(t_B\) is  

\[
0.125+0.25 = 0.375\text{ mile}.
\]

Bob finishes, so Dave’s speed doubles to \(4\) mph.

---

### 3.  From \(t_B\) onward (speed \(4\) mph)

Remaining distance to the 1‑mile mark:

\[
1-0.375 = 0.625\text{ mile}.
\]

Time needed at \(4\) mph:

\[
\Delta t = \frac{0.625}{4}=0.15625\text{ hr}.
\]

Thus Dave finishes at  

\[
t = t_B + \Delta t = 0.25 + 0.15625 = 0.40625\text{ hr}.
\]

Charlie would finish at \(t_C=0.5\) hr, after Dave has already crossed the line.

---

\[
0.40625\text{ hr}= \frac{13}{32}\text{ hr}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{13}{32}}
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
The only forbidden adjacent pairs are  

\[
ab \qquad\text{and}\qquad ac .
\]

Thus after an \(a\) the next letter cannot be \(b\) or \(c\); the only letter that may follow an \(a\) is another \(a\) (or the word may end).  

Consequently, once an \(a\) appears in the word, all later letters must also be \(a\).  
Hence every admissible word has the form  

\[
\underbrace{x_1x_2\ldots x_k}_{\text{each }x_i\in\{b,c\}} \;\underbrace{a a\ldots a}_{5-k\text{ times}},
\]

where \(k\) (the number of initial non‑\(a\) letters) can be any integer from \(0\) to \(5\).

For a fixed \(k\) there are \(2^k\) ways to choose the first \(k\) letters (each can be \(b\) or \(c\)).  
Summing over all possible \(k\):

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{5} 2^{k}=2^{0}+2^{1}+2^{2}+2^{3}+2^{4}+2^{5}
=1+2+4+8+16+32=63 .
\]

Thus the number of five‑letter words that avoid the substrings “ab’’ and “ac’’ is  

\[
\boxed{63}.
\]

subject: hmmt_feb_2026
sample_text:
The divisors of an integer \(n\) are listed in decreasing order  
\(d_1>d_2>\dots >d_k\).  
We need the sixth largest divisor to be \(6\); hence

\[
d_6 = 6 ,\qquad d_1=n .
\]

Thus there are exactly five divisors larger than \(6\).  
Let  

\[
L=\{d\in D(n):d<6\},\qquad |L|=a .
\]

Because \(6\mid n\), the numbers \(1,2,3\) are always in \(L\); hence \(a\ge 3\).

Each divisor \(d<6\) pairs with a distinct divisor \(\frac{n}{d}>6\).  
Therefore the number of divisors larger than \(6\) equals  

\[
1\;(\text{the divisor }n) + a\;(\text{partners of the }a\text{ small divisors}) + 1\;(\text{the partner of }6).
\]

We require this total to be \(5\); hence  

\[
1 + a + 1 = 5 \Longrightarrow a = 3 .
\]

But with \(a=3\) the small divisors are only \(\{1,2,3\}\).  
Their partners give the four proper divisors \(n/2,\,n/3,\,n/6\); we would still need one more divisor \(>6\), which would require another small divisor \(<6\).  
Thus \(a\) cannot be \(3\); the smallest possible value is \(a=4\).

Hence the set of divisors less than \(6\) must be \(\{1,2,3,4\}\); consequently \(4\mid n\) and \(5\nmid n\).  
With \(a=4\) the count of divisors of \(n\) is  

\[
\tau(n)=a+6=10 .
\]

So \(n\) must have exactly ten divisors, be divisible by \(12=2^{2}\cdot3\), and not be divisible by \(5\).

A number has ten divisors only when its prime‑factorisation is either  

\[
p^{9}\qquad\text{or}\qquad p^{4}q,
\]

with distinct primes \(p,q\).  
To contain the factor \(2^{2}\cdot3\) we must have  

\[
n = 2^{4}\cdot 3 = 48 .
\]

Indeed, \(\tau(48)=(4+1)(1+1)=10\) and the divisors of \(48\) are  

\[
1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,48 .
\]

Listed in decreasing order:

\[
48,24,16,12,8,6,4,3,2,1,
\]

so the sixth largest divisor is \(6\).

No other integer satisfies all the required conditions, so the sum of all such \(n\) is simply \(48\).

\[
\boxed{48}
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
The four roots are  

\[
r_{1,2}= -1\pm 2i ,\qquad
s_{1,2}= m\pm\sqrt{m^{2}-25}\;(=m\pm d ),
\]

where \(d=\sqrt{m^{2}-25}\).

Four points \(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},z_{4}\) are concyclic (or collinear) iff the cross–ratio
\[
\lambda=\frac{(z_{1}-z_{3})(z_{2}-z_{4})}{(z_{1}-z_{4})(z_{2}-z_{3})}
\]
is a real number.  
Take \(z_{1}=r_{1}, z_{2}=r_{2}, z_{3}=s_{1}, z_{4}=s_{2}\).

Set  

\[
a=-(m+1),\qquad d=\sqrt{m^{2}-25}.
\]

Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{1}-s_{1}&=a-d+2i,\\
r_{2}-s_{2}&=a+d-2i,\\
r_{1}-s_{2}&=a+d+2i,\\
r_{2}-s_{1}&=a-d-2i .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\lambda=\frac{(a-d+2i)(a+d-2i)}{(a+d+2i)(a-d-2i)}.
\]

Writing the numerator and denominator,

\[
\begin{aligned}
N&=(a^{2}-d^{2})+4+4i\,d,\\
D&=(a^{2}-d^{2})+4-4i\,d,
\end{aligned}
\]

so that  

\[
\lambda=\frac{S+ iT}{S- iT},\qquad 
S=(a^{2}-d^{2})+4,\; T=4d .
\]

For a complex number of the form \(\frac{S+iT}{S-iT}\) to be real we must have  

\[
\operatorname{Im}\lambda=0\iff ST=0 .
\]

Therefore the concyclicity condition is  

\[
\boxed{d=0}\quad\text{or}\quad\boxed{S=0}.
\]

---

### 1.  \(d=0\)

\(d=0\Longrightarrow m^{2}=25\Longrightarrow m=5\) or \(m=-5\).

---

### 2.  \(S=0\)

\(S=0\iff a^{2}-d^{2}+4=0\).

Since \(a=-(m+1)\) and \(d^{2}=m^{2}-25\),

\[
(m+1)^{2}-(m^{2}-25)+4=0
\Longrightarrow 2m+30=0
\Longrightarrow m=-15 .
\]

---

Hence the set \(U\) of all complex numbers \(m\) for which the four roots are concyclic is

\[
U=\{-15,\,5,\,-5\}.
\]

It consists of three isolated points; no non‑trivial curve appears.  
The total length (perimeter) of a finite union of points is zero.

\[
\boxed{0}
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
For the parabola  

\[
y=(x-a)^2\qquad (a=0,5,10,\dots ,45)
\]

the horizontal line \(y=k\) meets it where  

\[
(x-a)^2=k\;\Longrightarrow\;x-a=\pm\sqrt{k}.
\]

Let  

\[
s=\sqrt{k}>0 .
\]

For each centre \(a\) we obtain the two abscissas  

\[
x=a-s,\qquad x=a+s .
\]

Thus the set of intersection abscissas is  

\[
S=\{\,a\pm s\mid a\in\{0,5,10,\dots ,45\}\,\}.
\]

If the numbers \(a\pm s\) are all different, we would have \(20\) distinct points.  
Two points coincide when a right‑hand value from one parabola equals a left‑hand
value from another:

\[
a_1+s = a_2-s \;\Longrightarrow\; a_2-a_1 = 2s .
\]

Since the centers differ by multiples of \(5\), we need  

\[
2s =5m \qquad(m\in\{1,2,\dots ,9\}),
\]

i.e.  

\[
s = \frac{5m}{2}=2.5m .
\]

Take such an \(s\).  
For every pair of indices \(i\) and \(i+m\) (\(i=0,\dots ,9-m\)) we have the coincidence  

\[
(5i)+s = (5(i+m))-s .
\]

Hence the number of coincidences equals \(10-m\).  
Starting from the maximal \(20\) points, the number of distinct points is  

\[
20-(10-m)=10+m .
\]

We want \(10+m=19\), therefore \(m=9\).

Hence  

\[
s = 2.5\cdot 9 = 22.5=\frac{45}{2},
\qquad
k=s^{2} =\left(\frac{45}{2}\right)^{2}= \frac{2025}{4}.
\]

The line \(y=\dfrac{2025}{4}\) meets the ten parabolas in \(19\) distinct points.

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{2025}{4}}
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
For a positive integer \(n\) let  

\[
\tau(n)=\text{number of positive divisors of }n ,\qquad 
a(n)=\#\{d\mid d\mid n,\; d\le 100\}.
\]

A divisor \(d\) satisfies \(d\ge \dfrac{n}{100}\) iff the paired divisor
\(\dfrac{n}{d}\le 100\).  
Hence the number of “large’’ divisors (those \(\ge n/100\)) equals \(a(n)\).

The condition “strictly more than \(99\%\) of the divisors are \(<1\%\) of \(n\)’’ is  

\[
\frac{\tau(n)-a(n)}{\tau(n)}>0.99\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 
a(n)<0.01\,\tau(n).
\]

Thus we need  

\[
\tau(n)>100\,a(n). \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### The unavoidable small divisors

\(M\) must be a multiple of  

\[
2000 =2^{4}\,5^{3}.
\]

All divisors of \(2000\) that are \(\le 100\) are

\[
2^{i}5^{j}\quad (0\le i\le4,\;0\le j\le2)
\]

giving  

\[
a(2000)=5+5+3=13 .
\]

Any additional prime factor larger than \(100\) creates divisors
larger than \(100\); therefore for every integer \(M\) that is a multiple
of \(2000\) and whose extra prime factors are all \(>100\),

\[
a(M)=13. \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Making \(\tau(M)\) just large enough

From (1) and (2) we need  

\[
\tau(M)>1300 .
\]

Write the factorisation of \(M\) as  

\[
M = 2^{4}\,5^{3}\,p_{1}^{e_{1}}p_{2}^{e_{2}}\dots p_{k}^{e_{k}},
\qquad p_i>100 .
\]

Then  

\[
\tau(M)= (4+1)(3+1)\prod_{i=1}^{k}(e_i+1)=20\prod_{i=1}^{k}(e_i+1).
\]

We must choose the integers \(e_i+1\;( \ge 2)\) so that  

\[
20\prod_{i}(e_i+1)>1300\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 
\prod_{i}(e_i+1)>65 .
\]

The smallest possible product of integers \(\ge 2\) that exceeds \(65\) is  

\[
66 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 11 .
\]

Thus we can take three new primes \(p,q,r>100\) and use exponents  

\[
e_{1}=1,\qquad e_{2}=2,\qquad e_{3}=10,
\]

so that \((e_1+1)(e_2+1)(e_3+1)=2\cdot3\cdot11=66\).

Consequently  

\[
\tau(M)=20\cdot66 = 1320 .
\]

Because \(a(M)=13\), we have  

\[
\frac{\tau(M)-a(M)}{\tau(M)} = \frac{1320-13}{1320}
      = 1-\frac{13}{1320}=0.99015\ldots>0.99,
\]

so \(M\) is indeed imbalanced.

No smaller divisor count works: any \(\tau(M)\le 1319\) would give
\(\tau(M)\le 1300\) (since \(\tau(M)\) must be a multiple of \(20\)),
contradicting inequality (1). Hence \(1320\) is the minimum possible.

\[
\boxed{1320}
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
For a positive real \(x\) write  

\[
x = k+t ,\qquad k=\lfloor x\rfloor\ge 0,\; t\in[0,1).
\]

---

### 1.  Integer \(x\)  

If \(t=0\) (so \(x=k\ge 1\) is an integer) then  

\[
\lceil x\rceil+\lfloor x\rfloor = k+k=2k,
\qquad
x(\lceil x\rceil+\lfloor x\rfloor)=k\cdot 2k = 2k^{2}.
\]

Hence every integer of the form \(2k^{2}\;(k\ge 1)\) can be represented.

---

### 2.  Non‑integer \(x\)

If \(0<t<1\) then \(\lceil x\rceil = k+1,\ \lfloor x\rfloor = k\) and  

\[
\lceil x\rceil+\lfloor x\rfloor = 2k+1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
x(\lceil x\rceil+\lfloor x\rfloor)
  = (k+t)(2k+1)
  = k(2k+1) + (2k+1)t .
\]

Because \(t\) ranges over \((0,1)\), the expression assumes every value in the **open** interval  

\[
\bigl(k(2k+1),\ (k+1)(2k+1)\bigr)
 =\bigl(2k^{2}+k,\ 2k^{2}+3k+1\bigr) .
\]

Consequently the integers that arise from non‑integer \(x\) are  

\[
2k^{2}+k+1,\;2k^{2}+k+2,\dots ,\;2k^{2}+3k,
\]

a total of \(2k\) consecutive integers for each \(k\ge 1\).

---

### 3.  All representable integers

For each \(k\ge 1\) we obtain \(2k\) integers from the interval above and the single integer \(2k^{2}\) from the integer case.  
These sets are disjoint because the gap between the highest integer of the \(k\)-th interval and the lowest integer of the \((k+1)\)-st interval equals \(2k+4>0\).

Hence, up to a given \(K\),

\[
\#\{\text{representable integers}\}= \sum_{k=1}^{K} (2k+1)
= 2\sum_{k=1}^{K}k + K
= 2\cdot\frac{K(K+1)}{2}+K = K^{2}+2K .
\]

---

### 4.  Largest \(k\) needed for the range \(1\le n\le2025\)

The smallest integer contributed by the interval for a given \(k\) is  

\[
L_k = 2k^{2}+k+1 .
\]

We need \(L_k\le 2025\). Solving \(2k^{2}+k+1\le2025\) gives \(k\le 31\) (since for \(k=31\), \(L_{31}=1954\) and for \(k=32\), \(L_{32}=2081>2025\)).

Thus we consider \(k=1,2,\dots ,31\).  

All numbers contributed by these \(k\) are \(\le 2015\); the remaining integers \(2016,2017,\dots ,2025\) are not representable.

---

### 5.  Count of representable integers

\[
\#\text{representable}= \sum_{k=1}^{31}(2k+1)
= 31 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{31}k
= 31 + 2\cdot\frac{31\cdot32}{2}
= 31 + 992 = 1023 .
\]

---

### 6.  Non‑representable integers between 1 and 2025

\[
2025 - 1023 = 1002 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{1002}
\]

sample_text:
From  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a^2+ab+b^2 &=3(a+b) \quad &(1)\\
a^2+ac+c^2 &=3(a+c) \quad &(2)\\
b^2+bc+c^2 &=5(b+c)+1 \quad &(3)
\end{aligned}
\]

subtract \((1)\) from \((2)\):

\[
b(a+b)-c(a+c)=3(b-c)
\]
\[
(b-c)(a+b+c)=3(b-c)\Longrightarrow a+b+c=3 \qquad (A)
\]

Set \(c=3-a-b\) and denote \(S=a+b\).  
Equation \((1)\) gives  

\[
a^2+ab+b^2=3S\Longrightarrow S^{2}-ab=3S\Longrightarrow ab=S^{2}-3S. \tag{B}
\]

Using \(c=3-S\) in \((3)\) and simplifying with (B) yields  

\[
S-7+(a-b)=0\Longrightarrow a-b=7-S. \tag{C}
\]

From \(a+b=S\) and \(a-b=7-S\),

\[
a=\frac{(a+b)+(a-b)}{2}= \frac{S+7-S}{2}= \boxed{\frac{7}{2}} .
\]

(Indeed, with \(a=7/2\) we get \(b=\frac{-1\pm 3i\sqrt3}{4}\) and
\(c=3-a-b\), which satisfy all three given equations and are pairwise distinct.)

sample_text:
Place the triangle with  

\[
A=(0,0),\qquad B=(78,0),\qquad 
C=\left(\frac{1344}{13},\frac{560}{13}\right)
\]

(the side lengths satisfy \(AB=78,\;BC=50,\;CA=112\)).

---

### Vertices of the external squares  

For a side vector \(\vec v=(x,y)\) the outward (exterior) normal for a counter‑clockwise triangle is the clockwise rotation \((y,-x)\).

* **Square on \(AB\)** :  
  \(\vec{AB}=(78,0)\) → outward normal \((0,-78)\)  

  \[
  X=(78,-78),\qquad Y=(0,-78).
  \]

* **Square on \(BC\)** :  
  \(\vec{BC}=\Bigl(\frac{330}{13},\frac{560}{13}\Bigr)\) → outward normal \(\Bigl(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{330}{13}\Bigr)\)  

  \[
  P=C+\Bigl(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{330}{13}\Bigr)=\left(\frac{1904}{13},\frac{230}{13}\right),\qquad 
  Q=B+\Bigl(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{330}{13}\Bigr)=\left(\frac{1574}{13},-\frac{330}{13}\right).
  \]

* **Square on \(CA\)** :  
  \(\vec{CA}=(-\frac{1344}{13},-\frac{560}{13})\) (or \(\vec{AC}=(\frac{1344}{13},\frac{560}{13})\)) → outward normal \(\Bigl(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{1344}{13}\Bigr)\)  

  \[
  M=C+\Bigl(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{1344}{13}\Bigr)=\left(\frac{1904}{13},-\frac{784}{13}\right),\qquad 
  N=A+\Bigl(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{1344}{13}\Bigr)=\left(\frac{560}{13},-\frac{1344}{13}\right).
  \]

---

### Midpoints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{1}&=\text{midpoint of }MP
      =\left(\frac{1904}{13},\frac{-784/13+230/13}{2}\right)
      =\left(\frac{1904}{13},-\frac{277}{13}\right),\\[2mm]
L_{2}&=\text{midpoint of }QX
      =\left(\frac{1574/13+78}{2},\frac{-330/13-78}{2}\right)
      =\left(\frac{1294}{13},-\frac{672}{13}\right),\\[2mm]
L_{3}&=\text{midpoint of }NY
      =\left(\frac{560/13+0}{2},\frac{-1344/13-78}{2}\right)
      =\left(\frac{280}{13},-\frac{1179}{13}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Area of \(\triangle L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}\)

Write the coordinates with a common denominator \(13\):

\[
L_{1}=\left(\frac{1904}{13},-\frac{277}{13}\right),\;
L_{2}=\left(\frac{1294}{13},-\frac{672}{13}\right),\;
L_{3}=\left(\frac{280}{13},-\frac{1179}{13}\right).
\]

Using the shoelace formula (the factor \(\frac1{13^2}\) comes from the scaling):

\[
\begin{aligned}
S &=\;1904(-672)+1294(-1179)+280(-277)\\
  &\quad -\bigl[(-277)1294+(-672)280+(-1179)1904\bigr]\\
  &= -91\,260 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\text{Area}= \frac12\frac{|S|}{13^{2}}
           =\frac12\frac{91\,260}{169}= \frac{45\,630}{169}=270.
\]

\[
\boxed{270}
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
In the \(3\times3\) array of unit squares the vertices form a \(4\times4\) lattice.  
Give each vertex coordinates \((i,j)\;(0\le i,j\le 3)\).  
In a cell with lower‑left corner \((i,j)\) we may draw

* the diagonal \((i,j)\leftrightarrow(i+1,j+1)\)   (call it the **even** diagonal when \(i+j\) is even), or  
* the diagonal \((i,j+1)\leftrightarrow(i+1,j)\)   (the **odd** diagonal).

For each cell exactly one diagonal is drawn, therefore each cell contributes **one edge among the even‑parity vertices** and **one edge among the odd‑parity vertices**.  
The bottom‑left vertex \((0,0)\) and the top‑right vertex \((3,3)\) are both even, so a path between them can use only the edges that connect even vertices.

Hence the problem reduces to:

*There are 9 possible edges between the eight even vertices; each cell decides independently whether its even edge is present or not.  
How many subsets of these 9 edges contain a path from \((0,0)\) to \((3,3)\)?*

---

### The graph of even vertices  

The even vertices are  

\[
\begin{array}{c}
E_0=(0,0),\;E_1=(0,2),\;E_2=(1,1),\;E_3=(1,3),\\[2pt]
E_4=(2,0),\;E_5=(2,2),\;E_6=(3,1),\;E_7=(3,3).
\end{array}
\]

The nine possible even edges (one per cell) are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
e_1 &:E_0E_2, & e_2 &:E_1E_2, & e_3 &:E_1E_3,\\
e_4 &:E_2E_4, & e_5 &:E_2E_5, & e_6 &:E_3E_5,\\
e_7 &:E_4E_6, & e_8 &:E_5E_6, & e_9 &:E_5E_7 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Observe that \(E_0\) and \(E_7\) are each incident to only one edge:
\(E_0\) only to \(e_1\) and \(E_7\) only to \(e_9\).
Therefore any connecting subgraph must contain **both** \(e_1\) and \(e_9\).

With \(e_1\) and \(e_9\) forced, a path from \((0,0)\) to \((3,3)\) exists iff the vertices
\(E_2\) and \(E_5\) are connected in the subgraph formed by the remaining seven edges
\[
e_2,e_3,e_4,e_5,e_6,e_7,e_8 .
\]

---

### When are \(E_2\) and \(E_5\) disconnected?

The three possible ways to join \(E_2\) to \(E_5\) are

* directly via \(e_5\);
* via the “upper” chain \(E_2\!-\!E_1\!-\!E_3\!-\!E_5\) (edges \(e_2,e_3,e_6\));
* via the “lower” chain \(E_2\!-\!E_4\!-\!E_6\!-\!E_5\) (edges \(e_4,e_7,e_8\)).

Hence \(E_2\) and \(E_5\) are **disconnected** exactly when  

* \(e_5\) is absent, **and**  
* at least one of \(e_2,e_3,e_6\) is absent, **and**  
* at least one of \(e_4,e_7,e_8\) is absent.

Fix \(e_5=0\).  
Among the other six edges there are \(2^6=64\) possibilities.
Count those that violate the two “at least one missing’’ conditions:

* all of \(e_2,e_3,e_6\) present: \(2^3=8\) choices for the remaining three edges;
* all of \(e_4,e_7,e_8\) present: another \(8\);
* both groups present simultaneously: \(1\) choice.

Thus the number with **at least one whole group present** is \(8+8-1=15\).

Consequently the number with **neither** group completely present is  

\[
64-15=49 .
\]

So, with \(e_1\) and \(e_9\) forced, there are \(49\) subsets of the remaining edges that leave \(E_2\) and \(E_5\) disconnected, and therefore  

\[
128-49=79
\]

subsets that **do** connect them.

---

### Total number of valid diagonal drawings

Every choice of a subset of the nine even edges corresponds to exactly one way of drawing the diagonals in the nine cells.  
Hence the number of diagonal configurations that provide a continuous path from the bottom‑left vertex to the top‑right vertex equals the number of connected edge subsets we have just found:

\[
\boxed{79}
\]

subject: hmmt_feb_2026
sample_text:
Let  

\[
k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor ,\qquad 
A=(k)!\;^{\,n!}.
\]

The condition is  

\[
n\mid A+450 .\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What happens for a prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\)?

*If \(p\le k\):* then \(p\mid(k)!\); hence \(A\equiv0\pmod p\).  
From (1) we obtain \(p\mid 450\).

Thus **every prime \(\le k\) that divides \(n\) must be a divisor of \(450\); i.e.**
\[
p\in\{2,3,5\}.
\tag{2}
\]

*If \(p>k\):* then \(p\nmid(k)!\), so \((k)!\) is invertible modulo \(p\).  
Since \(p-1\le n-1\) we have \(p-1\mid n!\).  By Fermat,
\[
(k)!^{\,p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\Longrightarrow
(k)!^{\,n!}\equiv1\pmod p .
\]

Equation (1) now gives  

\[
1+450\equiv0\pmod p\Longrightarrow p\mid 451=11\cdot41 .
\tag{3}
\]

Hence a prime factor of \(n\) larger than \(k\) can only be \(11\) or \(41\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Eliminate the option \(p=11\).

If \(p=11>k\) then we would need \(k<11\); this forces \(n<11^{2}=121\).
All such \(n\) are \(\le 120<450\), so they cannot beat the later candidates.
Thus the only viable large prime factor is \(p=41\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Consequences of having the factor \(41\)

If \(41\mid n\) we must have \(k<41\); otherwise \(41\le k\) and,
by the argument for \(p\le k\), \(41\) would have to divide \(450\), which it
does not.  Hence  

\[
k<41\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n<41^{2}=1681 .
\tag{4}
\]

Write \(n=41\cdot d\).  
All prime divisors of \(d\) are \(\le k\), so by (2) they belong to \(\{2,3,5\}\);
consequently  

\[
d\mid 2\cdot3^{2}\cdot5^{2}=450 .
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Maximal \(n\)

From (4) we need \(41d<1681\), i.e. \(d<41\).  
Using (5), the largest divisor of \(450\) that is \(<41\) is  

\[
d_{\max}=30 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
n_{\max}=41\cdot30=1230 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Verification

For \(n=1230\) we have \(k=\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor =35\).

* Primes \(2,3,5\) divide \((35)!\), so \((35)!^{\,1230!}\equiv0\pmod{2,3,5}\);
  consequently \( (35)!^{\,1230!}+450\equiv450\equiv0\pmod{2,3,5}\).

* \(41>k\); \((35)!\) is invertible modulo \(41\) and \(40\mid1230!\), hence  
  \((35)!^{\,1230!}\equiv1\pmod{41}\).  
  Thus \((35)!^{\,1230!}+450\equiv1+450=451\equiv0\pmod{41}\).

Thus \(1230\mid (35)!^{\,1230!}+450\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  No larger \(n\)

* If \(n\) has **no** prime factor \(>k\), then all its prime factors must be
  among \(\{2,3,5\}\) and \(n\mid450\); the largest such \(n\) is \(450\).

* If \(n\) contains a prime factor \(>k\), it must be \(41\) and satisfy
  \(n<1681\). The maximal value under this restriction is the \(1230\) found
  above.

Hence the largest positive integer satisfying the required divisibility is  

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]

subject: smt_2025
sample_text:
The divisor function \(\tau(n)\) satisfies  

\[
\tau(n)=\prod (e_i+1)
\]

when \(n=\prod p_i^{\,e_i}\).

Because the product \(ab\) has exactly \(15\) divisors,  

\[
\tau(ab)=15=3\cdot5 .
\]

Hence the exponent pattern of \(ab\) must be one of  

* a single prime power: \(p^{14}\)  \((e_1+1)=15\), or  
* two distinct primes: \(p^{4}q^{2}\)  \((e_1+1)=5,\;(e_2+1)=3\).

All primes must be odd, otherwise the numbers would be even.

---

### 1. Case \(ab=p^{14}\)

Write \(a=p^{k},\;b=p^{14-k}\) (\(0\le k\le14\)).  
The sum is  

\[
S(k)=p^{k}+p^{14-k},
\]

which is minimal when \(k=7\), giving  

\[
S_{\min}=2p^{7}.
\]

With the smallest odd prime \(p=3\),

\[
S_{\min}=2\cdot3^{7}=2\cdot2187=4374.
\]

---

### 2. Case \(ab=p^{4}q^{2}\) with distinct odd primes \(p\neq q\)

Let  

\[
a=p^{i}q^{j},\qquad b=p^{4-i}q^{2-j},
\qquad 0\le i\le4,\;0\le j\le2 .
\]

Then  

\[
S(i,j)=p^{i}q^{j}+p^{4-i}q^{2-j}.
\]

The product’s square‑root is \(p^{2}q\); the sum is smallest when the two factors are as close as possible, i.e. when \(i=2,\;j=1\).  
Thus

\[
S_{\min}=2p^{2}q .
\]

To minimise \(2p^{2}q\) we choose the smallest odd prime for the larger exponent, namely \(p=3\) and the next smallest odd prime for the smaller exponent, \(q=5\):

\[
S_{\min}=2\cdot3^{2}\cdot5=2\cdot9\cdot5=90.
\]

Checking this choice:

\[
a=b=3^{2}\cdot5=45,\qquad ab=3^{4}\cdot5^{2}=2025,
\]
\[
\tau(ab)=(4+1)(2+1)=5\cdot3=15,
\]

so the conditions are satisfied.

All other distributions of the exponents (or larger primes) give larger sums, as a quick enumeration confirms.

---

The smallest possible sum of the two odd numbers is therefore  

\[
\boxed{90}.
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
From  

\[
(10a+b)(10a+c)=a+\frac1a ,\qquad 
(10b+a)(10b+c)=b+\frac1b ,\qquad 
(10c+a)(10c+b)=c+\frac1c 
\]

expand the first equality:

\[
100a^{2}+10a(b+c)+bc=a+\frac1a .
\]

Hence  

\[
bc=a+\frac1a-100a^{2}-10a(b+c)
   =a+\frac1a-90a^{2}-10a(a+b+c). \tag{1}
\]

Analogously  

\[
\begin{aligned}
ac&=b+\frac1b-90b^{2}-10b(a+b+c),\\
ab&=c+\frac1c-90c^{2}-10c(a+b+c). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

Let  

\[
S_{1}=a+b+c,\qquad S_{2}=ab+bc+ca,\qquad S_{3}=abc .
\]

Using (1)–(2) we have  

\[
bc=S_{3}/a = a+\frac1a-90a^{2}-10aS_{1},
\]
so after multiplying by \(a\),

\[
S_{3}=a^{2}+1-90a^{3}-10a^{2}S_{1}.
\]

Thus each of \(a,b,c\) satisfies  

\[
90x^{3}+(10S_{1}-1)x^{2}+(S_{3}-1)=0. \tag{3}
\]

Since the three numbers are distinct roots of a cubic, the monic cubic with
roots \(a,b,c\) is  

\[
x^{3}-S_{1}x^{2}+S_{2}x-S_{3}=0.
\]

Multiplying by \(90\) to match the leading coefficient of (3) and equating
coefficients gives  

\[
\begin{cases}
-90S_{1}=10S_{1}-1,\\[2pt]
90S_{2}=0,\\[2pt]
-90S_{3}=S_{3}-1 .
\end{cases}
\]

Solving,

\[
S_{1}=\frac1{100},\qquad S_{2}=0,\qquad S_{3}=\frac1{91}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
abc=S_{3}= \boxed{\dfrac{1}{91}}.
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
The black squares can be regarded as edges of a bipartite graph whose two parts are the rows and the columns of the grid.  
When the ant walks, it can turn only on black squares; this means that a closed walk for the ant corresponds exactly to a cycle in this bipartite graph (a rectangle formed by two rows and two columns).  

Hence a coloring is **simple** iff the set of black squares forms an acyclic subgraph (a forest) of the complete bipartite graph \(K_{2024,2024}\).  
The coloring is **maximal simple** when no additional black square can be added without creating a cycle; this occurs precisely when the forest is a spanning tree of \(K_{2024,2024}\).

The number of spanning trees of the complete bipartite graph \(K_{a,b}\) is known (Kirchhoff’s theorem):

\[
\tau(K_{a,b}) = a^{\,b-1}\, b^{\,a-1}.
\]

Taking \(a=b=2024\),

\[
\tau(K_{2024,2024}) = 2024^{2024-1}\, 2024^{2024-1}=2024^{2\cdot2024-2}=2024^{4046}.
\]

Thus the number of maximal simple colorings of the \(2024\times2024\) grid equals \(2024^{4046}\).

\[
\boxed{2024^{4046}}
\]

sample_text:
Let  

\[
a=\log_x y,\qquad b=\log_y z,\qquad c=\log_z x .
\]

Then  

\[
\begin{cases}
a+b+c=8,\\[2pt]
\log_{\log_y x}z=-3,\\[2pt]
\log_z y+\log_x z=16 .
\end{cases}
\]

---

### 1.  Express the second equation in \(a,b,c\)

\[
\log_y x=\frac{1}{\log_x y}=\frac1a .
\]

Hence  

\[
\log_{\frac1a}z=-3\Longrightarrow \Big(\frac1a\Big)^{-3}=z\Longrightarrow z=a^{3}.
\]

---

### 2.  Express the third equation in \(a,b,c\)

\[
\log_z y =\log_z (x^{a}) = a\log_z x = a c,
\qquad
\log_x z =\log_x (y^{b}) = b\log_x y = a b .
\]

So  

\[
ac+ab = a(b+c)=16. \tag{1}
\]

---

### 3.  Relate \(a,b,c\) using the definitions of the logs  

From  

\[
y=x^{a},\quad z=y^{b}=x^{ab},\quad x=z^{c}=x^{abc},
\]

we obtain  

\[
abc=1. \tag{2}
\]

---

### 4.  System in \(a,b,c\)

\[
\begin{cases}
a+b+c=8,\\[2pt]
a(b+c)=16,\\[2pt]
abc=1 .
\end{cases}
\]

From \(a(b+c)=16\) we have \(b+c=\dfrac{16}{a}\).  
Using \(a+b+c=8\),

\[
a+\frac{16}{a}=8\Longrightarrow a^{2}-8a+16=0\Longrightarrow (a-4)^{2}=0,
\]

so  

\[
a=4.
\]

Then  

\[
b+c=8-a=4,\qquad bc=\frac{1}{a}= \frac14.
\]

Thus \(b,c\) are the roots of \(t^{2}-4t+\frac14=0\),

\[
b,c =\frac{4\pm\sqrt{15}}{2}=2\pm\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.
\]

(Their order is irrelevant for the problem.)

---

### 5.  Find \(z\)

From step 1, \(z=a^{3}=4^{3}=64\).

All equations are satisfied:

* \(\log_x y =4\), \(\log_y x =\frac14\), so \(\log_{\,\frac14}64=-3\);
* \(\log_z y =ac=4\cdot\!\bigl(2-\frac{\sqrt{15}}2\bigr)\), \(\log_x z=ab\), giving \(ac+ab=16\);
* and \(a+b+c=8\).

\[
\boxed{64}
\]

sample_text:
The two external common tangents intersect at a point \(H\).  
Let the angle between them be \(\theta\) and set \( \beta=\frac{\theta}{2}\).  

For the intersection point \(P\) of the circles we have  

\[
\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell_1)=R\sin(\alpha+\beta)=3,\qquad 
\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell_2)=R\sin(\alpha-\beta)=12,
\]

so  

\[
\frac{\sin(\alpha-\beta)}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}=4
      \Longrightarrow \frac{\tan\alpha-\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha+\tan\beta}=4
      \Longrightarrow 3\tan\alpha+5\tan\beta=0 .
\]

Hence \(\tan\alpha= -\dfrac{5}{3}\tan\beta\).

Put \(y=\tan\beta\); then  

\[
\sin\theta =\frac{2y}{1+y^{2}}, \qquad 
\cos\theta =\frac{1-y^{2}}{1+y^{2}},\qquad 
\sec\theta =S=\frac{1+y^{2}}{1-y^{2}} .
\]

Let the distances from \(H\) to the points of tangency of \(\Gamma_1\) be \(t_1\) and to those of \(\Gamma_2\) be \(t_2\;(t_2>t_1)\).
A short computation (using that both circles are tangent to the two lines) shows that

\[
t_1+t_2=\frac{30S}{\tan\theta},\qquad 
t_2-t_1=\sqrt{\frac{288S}{S+1}} .
\]

The area of quadrilateral \(U_1U_2V_2V_1\) equals  

\[
\frac12\sin\theta\;(t_2-t_1)(t_2+t_1)
 =\frac12\frac{\tan\theta}{S}\,(t_2-t_1)(t_2+t_1)
 =180\sqrt{1+y^{2}} .
\tag{1}
\]

Now use the given chord length \(PQ=10\).  
The line joining the centers of the circles is perpendicular to the chord, and the
distance from \(P\) to that line is \(\dfrac{PQ}{2}=5\).  From the geometry
described above this distance equals \(\dfrac{9}{2}\sqrt{1+y^{2}}\); hence  

\[
\frac{9}{2}\sqrt{1+y^{2}} =5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sqrt{1+y^{2}}=\frac{10}{9}.
\]

Substituting this value into (1),

\[
\text{Area}=180\cdot\frac{10}{9}=200 .
\]

\[
\boxed{200}
\]

sample_text:
The condition \(|z|=1\) lets us write \(z=e^{i\theta}\) with \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\).  
Divide the given polynomial by \(z^{4}\):

\[
\frac{z^{8}+iz^{6}-(1+i)z^{5}+(1-i)z^{3}+iz^{2}-1}{z^{4}}
= z^{4}+iz^{2}-(1+i)z+(1-i)z^{-1}+iz^{-2}-z^{-4}=0 .
\]

Using \(z=e^{i\theta}\) and the identities  

\[
z^{k}+z^{-k}=2\cos(k\theta),\qquad 
z^{k}-z^{-k}=2i\sin(k\theta),
\]

the equation becomes  

\[
2i\sin(4\theta)+2i\cos(2\theta)-2i\bigl(\sin\theta+\cos\theta\bigr)=0,
\]

or  

\[
\boxed{\sin(4\theta)+\cos(2\theta)=\sin\theta+\cos\theta } .
\]

Rewrite the left–hand side with sum‑to‑product formulas:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sin4\theta-\sin\theta &=2\cos\frac{5\theta}{2}\sin\frac{3\theta}{2},\\
\cos2\theta-\cos\theta &=-2\sin\frac{3\theta}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
2\sin\frac{3\theta}{2}\bigl(\cos\frac{5\theta}{2}-\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\bigr)=0 .
\]

Thus either  

1. \(\displaystyle \sin\frac{3\theta}{2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta=\frac{2k\pi}{3}\),  
   giving \(\theta=0,\; \frac{2\pi}{3}\) in \([0,\pi)\);  

or  

2. \(\displaystyle \cos\frac{5\theta}{2}=\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\).

Since \(\sin x=\cos\bigl(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\bigr)\), we have  

\[
\cos\frac{5\theta}{2}= \cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\theta}{2}\Bigr) .
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{5\theta}{2}= \pm\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\theta}{2}\Bigr)+2\pi n .
\]

These give  

\[
\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}+ \frac{2\pi}{3}n \quad\text{or}\quad \theta = -\frac{\pi}{4}+\pi n .
\]

Restricting to \([0,\pi)\) yields  

\[
\theta = \frac{\pi}{6},\; \frac{5\pi}{6},\; \frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]

Collecting all distinct solutions in \([0,\pi)\):

\[
\theta = 0,\; \frac{\pi}{6},\; \frac{2\pi}{3},\; \frac{3\pi}{4},\; \frac{5\pi}{6}.
\]

Finally, the sum of these angles is  

\[
0+\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2\pi}{3}+\frac{3\pi}{4}+\frac{5\pi}{6}
= \frac{0+2+8+9+10}{12}\pi = \frac{29\pi}{12}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{29\pi}{12}}
\]

sample_text:
The optimal strategy for Cubey is to move along a shortest path, which in a grid is a path of length equal to the Manhattan (ℓ₁) distance between the starting unit cube and the fish’s unit cube.

Because the coordinates in each of the four dimensions are independent, the expected Manhattan distance is  

\[
E[\text{distance}] = 4 \times E\bigl[|X-Y|\bigr],
\]

where \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent uniform random variables on \(\{0,1,2,3\}\).

---

### Compute \(E[|X-Y|]\)

All ordered pairs \((X,Y)\) are equally likely (16 possibilities).

| \(d=|X-Y|\) | Number of ordered pairs |
|------------|------------------------|
| 0 | 4 |
| 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 2 |

\[
E[|X-Y|] = \frac{0\cdot4 + 1\cdot6 + 2\cdot4 + 3\cdot2}{16}
          = \frac{6+8+6}{16}
          = \frac{20}{16}
          = \frac{5}{4}.
\]

---

### Expected Manhattan distance

\[
E[\text{distance}] = 4 \times \frac{5}{4} = 5.
\]

Thus the expected time (in seconds) for Cubey to catch the fish is  

\[
\boxed{5}.
\]

sample_text:
The prime factorisation of  

\[
9! = 1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots 9 = 2^{7}\,3^{4}\,5^{1}\,7^{1}
\]

A divisor of \(9!\) can be written as  

\[
d = 2^{a}3^{b}5^{c}7^{e},\qquad 
0\le a\le 7,\;0\le b\le 4,\;c\in\{0,1\},\;e\in\{0,1\}.
\]

For \(d\) to have units digit \(1\) we need  

\[
d\equiv 1\pmod{10}.
\]

Since \(10=2\cdot5\), this requires  

\[
d\equiv 1\pmod{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\equiv 1\pmod{5}.
\]

* Mod \(2\): a divisor ending in \(1\) is odd, hence \(a=0\).
* Mod \(5\): if \(c=1\) the divisor is a multiple of \(5\) and cannot be \(\equiv1\pmod5\).  
  Thus \(c=0\).

Now  

\[
d = 3^{b}7^{e},\qquad 0\le b\le4,\;e\in\{0,1\}.
\]

Compute residues modulo \(5\):

\[
3^{b}\pmod5:\; 1,3,4,2,1 \quad (b=0,1,2,3,4)
\]
\[
7^{e}\pmod5:\; 1\;(e=0),\;2\;(e=1)
\]

We need \(3^{b}7^{e}\equiv1\pmod5\).

* If \(e=0\) (\(7^{e}\equiv1\)), we require \(3^{b}\equiv1\pmod5\) → \(b=0\) or \(b=4\).
* If \(e=1\) (\(7^{e}\equiv2\)), we need \(3^{b}\equiv3\pmod5\) → \(b=1\).

Thus the admissible exponent pairs \((b,e)\) are  

\[
(0,0),\;(4,0),\;(1,1).
\]

Corresponding divisors:

\[
d_1 = 3^{0}7^{0}=1,\qquad
d_2 = 3^{4}7^{0}=81,\qquad
d_3 = 3^{1}7^{1}=21.
\]

All end with digit \(1\) and indeed divide \(9!\).

Sum of these divisors:

\[
1+81+21 = 103.
\]

\[
\boxed{103}
\]

sample_text:
The operation preserves the product of the two chosen numbers, since  

\[
a\cdot b = \gcd (a,b)\;\operatorname{lcm}(a,b).
\]

Hence the product of all numbers on the board never changes.  
Starting with  

\[
1,2,\dots ,2100,
\]

the total product is \(P = 1\cdot 2\cdot\ldots\cdot 2100\).

Whenever Mark picks two **coprime** numbers \(a\) and \(b\) we obtain  

\[
\gcd (a,b)=1,\qquad \operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=ab .
\]

Thus a coprime pair creates a new “1” while moving all prime factors of the pair into a single number.  
By repeatedly pairing coprime numbers, all prime factors can be gathered into one single number while producing a 1 for each pair that was used.

Since there are 2100 numbers in total, Mark can continue this process until only one number remains that contains **all** prime factors (i.e. it equals the original product \(P\)), and the remaining \(2100-1=2099\) numbers are all equal to \(1\).

At this point any further move would involve a pair \((1,1)\) or \((1,P)\) or \((P,P)\); in each case the pair already satisfies “one divides the other”, so the board no longer changes. Consequently the process must stop here, and this configuration is the unique final configuration reachable from the initial set.

In the final board the numbers, written in increasing order, are

\[
\underbrace{1,1,\dots ,1}_{2099\text{ times}},\;P .
\]

The \(2026^{\text{th}}\) smallest number is therefore \(1\).

The number \(1\) has exactly one positive divisor.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

sample_text:
The recurrence can be rewritten without the square‑root.

\[
a_{n+1}=\frac{5a_n+\sqrt{21a_n^{2}+4}}{2}
\Longrightarrow
\left(2a_{n+1}-5a_n\right)^2=21a_n^{2}+4
\]

\[
\Longrightarrow a_{n+1}^{2}-5a_n a_{n+1}+a_n^{2}=1.
\tag{1}
\]

Dividing (1) by \(a_n a_{n+1}\),

\[
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}+ \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}-5=\frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}.
\tag{2}
\]

Let  

\[
r_n=\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\qquad (n\ge 1).
\]

Using \(a_{n+1}=5a_n-a_{n-1}\) (which follows from (1)) we get  

\[
r_n=5-\frac{1}{r_{n-1}},\qquad r_1=\frac{a_2}{a_1}= \frac{24}{5}.
\tag{3}
\]

From (2),

\[
\frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}=r_n+\frac{1}{r_n}-5.
\]

But by (3),

\[
r_{n}+\frac{1}{r_n}-5 = -\bigl(r_{n+1}-r_n\bigr)= r_n-r_{n+1}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}} = r_n-r_{n+1},
\]

so the series telescopes:

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}
   = \bigl(r_1-r_2\bigr)+\bigl(r_2-r_3\bigr)+\dots+\bigl(r_N-r_{N+1}\bigr)
   = r_1-r_{N+1}.
\]

The limit of \(r_n\) satisfies \(r=5-\dfrac{1}{r}\), i.e.  

\[
r^2-5r+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2}
\]

(the larger root, because \(r_1=24/5>4\)).  
Thus

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}
   = r_1-\frac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2}
   = \frac{24}{5}-\frac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2}
   = \frac{48-(25+5\sqrt{21})}{10}
   = \frac{23-5\sqrt{21}}{10}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{23-5\sqrt{21}}{10}}
\]

subject: hmmt_nov_2025
sample_text:
The positions of Jacob \((x_J,y_J)\) and Bojac \((x_B,y_B)\) each lie in the \(8\times 8\) board, so there are at most  

\[
64\cdot 64 = 4096
\]

ordered pairs of positions.

The four possible instructions act on the four coordinates as  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Instruction} & (x_J,y_J,x_B,y_B) \longrightarrow  \\ \hline
N & (x_J,\,y_J+1,\,x_B-1,\,y_B) \\[2pt]
S & (x_J,\,y_J-1,\,x_B+1,\,y_B) \\[2pt]
E & (x_J+1,\,y_J,\,x_B,\,y_B+1) \\[2pt]
W & (x_J-1,\,y_J,\,x_B,\,y_B-1)
\end{array}
\]

(If a move would leave the board, the corresponding coordinate stays unchanged.)

From any state we can independently adjust each coordinate:

* To change \(x_J\) we use \(E\) or \(W\); when Jacob is at the rightmost (resp. leftmost) column the move leaves him in place while still moving \(y_B\). Hence \(x_J\) can be set to any column while \(y_B\) can be tuned arbitrarily by extra edge moves.

* To change \(y_J\) we use \(N\) or \(S\); analogously, when Jacob is at the top (resp. bottom) row the move only changes \(x_B\). Thus \(y_J\) can be set arbitrarily and \(x_B\) can be tuned.

By alternating these operations we can move from any starting quadruple \((x_J,y_J,x_B,y_B)\) to any other quadruple of board cells. Consequently the directed graph of states is **strongly connected**: from a suitable starting position we can visit every one of the \(4096\) possible ordered pairs.

Hence the largest number of distinct ordered pairs that can appear during a single sequence of instructions equals the total number of states.

\[
\boxed{4096}
\]

sample_text:
For a prime \(p=23\) Lucas’ theorem gives  

\[
\binom{n}{20}\pmod{23}= \binom{n_0}{20}\pmod{23},
\]

where \(n=n_0+ n_1\cdot23+\cdots\) is the base‑\(23\) expansion of \(n\) and \(0\le n_0\le 22\).
Since \(20<23\), the higher digits contribute a factor \(\binom{n_i}{0}=1\).  
Thus \(f(n)\) depends only on \(r=n\bmod 23\):

* If \(0\le r\le 19\), then \(\binom{r}{20}=0\) ⇒ \(f(n)=0\).
* If \(r=20\), \(\displaystyle f(n)=\binom{20}{20}=1\).
* If \(r=21\), \(\displaystyle f(n)=\binom{21}{20}=21\).
* If \(r=22\), \(\displaystyle f(n)=\binom{22}{20}= \binom{22}{2}=231\equiv1\pmod{23}\).

Hence  

\[
f(n)=\begin{cases}
0,& r=0,1,\dots ,19,\\[2pt]
1,& r=20\text{ or }22,\\[2pt]
21,& r=21.
\end{cases}
\]

---

### Counting the residues from \(20\) to \(2023\)

Number of terms:

\[
2023-20+1 = 2004.
\]

A full cycle of residues modulo \(23\) has length \(23\) and contributes a sum  

\[
1+21+1 = 23 .
\]

\[
2004 = 23\cdot 87 + 3,
\]

so there are \(87\) complete cycles and the remaining three terms correspond to residues
\(20,21,22\) (the first three residues of the next cycle).

Thus the total sum is  

\[
87\cdot 23 + (1+21+1)= 87\cdot 23 + 23 = 88\cdot 23 = 2024.
\]

\[
\boxed{2024}
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
Let  

\[
x=\varepsilon _1 u,\qquad y=\varepsilon _2 v ,\qquad 
\varepsilon _1,\varepsilon _2\in\{+1,-1\},\; u,v\in[0,1].
\]

Because \(x,y\) are uniform on \([-1,1]\), the pair \((u,v)\) is uniform on the unit
square \([0,1]^2\) (density \(1\)).  
For each \((u,v)\) there are four sign choices, each occurring with probability
\(\tfrac14\).

---

### 1.  Express the inequality in terms of \(u,v\).

\[
|x|+|y|+1 = u+v+1 .
\]

Let \(s=x+y=\varepsilon _1u+\varepsilon _2v\).

\[
\min\{|x+y+1|,\;|x+y-1|\}= \min\{|s+1|,\;|s-1|\}= \bigl|\,|s|-1\bigr|.
\]

Hence the condition is  

\[
u+v+1\le 3\bigl|\,|s|-1\bigr|.
\]

---

### 2.  Dependence on the signs

*If the signs are the same* (\(\varepsilon _1=\varepsilon _2\)):
\[
|s|=u+v,\qquad\text{so}\qquad
u+v+1\le 3|u+v-1|.
\tag{A}
\]

*If the signs are opposite* (\(\varepsilon _1\neq\varepsilon _2\)):
\[
|s|=|u-v|,\qquad\text{so}\qquad
u+v+1\le 3\bigl(1-|u-v|\bigr).
\tag{B}
\]

Thus we need the areas in the unit square where (A) and (B) hold.

---

### 3.  Area for the same‑sign case (A)

Let \(t=u+v\;(0\le t\le 2)\).  
Inequality (A) becomes  

\[
t+1\le 3|t-1|.
\]

*If \(t\ge1\):* \(\;t+1\le 3(t-1)\Rightarrow t\ge2\).  
*If \(t\le1\):* \(\;t+1\le 3(1-t)\Rightarrow t\le\frac12\).

Hence the admissible region is \(t\le\frac12\) (the tiny triangle at the
origin) together with the single point \((1,1)\), which has zero area.
The triangle has legs \(\frac12\), so  

\[
\text{area}_A=\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac18 .
\]

---

### 4.  Area for the opposite‑sign case (B)

Rewrite (B):

\[
u+v+1\le 3-3|u-v| \Longrightarrow 
3|u-v|\le 2-(u+v) .
\tag{1}
\]

Because the condition is symmetric in \(u\) and \(v\), consider the part
\(v\ge u\) and double the result.

With \(v\ge u\) we have \(|u-v|=v-u\).
Inequality (1) gives  

\[
3(v-u)\le 2-u-v\Longrightarrow 4v\le 2+2u\Longrightarrow 
v\le\frac{1+u}{2}.
\]

Thus for each \(u\in[0,1]\),

\[
u\le v\le\frac{1+u}{2},
\]

which exists because \(\frac{1+u}{2}\ge u\) for \(u\le1\).

The length of this interval is \(\displaystyle \frac{1-u}{2}\).
Hence the area in the half‑square \(v\ge u\) is  

\[
\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1-u}{2}\,du
= \frac12\Bigl[u-\frac{u^{2}}2\Bigr]_{0}^{1}
= \frac14 .
\]

Doubling for the symmetric part \(u\ge v\),

\[
\text{area}_B = 2\cdot\frac14 = \frac12 .
\]

---

### 5.  Combine the four sign possibilities

Two sign choices give case (A) and two give case (B).  
Therefore the overall probability is  

\[
P =\frac14\bigl(2\,\text{area}_A+2\,\text{area}_B\bigr)
    =\frac12\bigl(\text{area}_A+\text{area}_B\bigr)
    =\frac12\left(\frac18+\frac12\right)
    =\frac{5}{16}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\frac{5}{16}}
\]

subject: cmimc_2025
sample_text:
The multiples of \(77\) less than \(1\,000\,000\) are  

\[
77,\,154,\,231,\dots ,\,77\cdot 12987 = 999\,999 ,
\]

so there are  

\[
N = 12987
\]

such numbers.  

For any fixed decimal position (units, tens, …, hundred‑thousands) the digit in that position repeats every \(10^{k+1}\) numbers (\(k=0,1,\dots ,5\)).  
Since \(\gcd(77,10^{k+1})=1\), the residues \(77,154,231,\dots\) modulo \(10^{k+1}\) form a permutation of the numbers \(0,1,\dots ,10^{k+1}-1\).

Hence, in each position every digit occurs either  

\[
\Big\lfloor \frac{N}{10}\Big\rfloor =1298 \quad\text{or}\quad 
\Big\lceil \frac{N}{10}\Big\rceil =1299
\]

times, and exactly seven digits occur \(1299\) times while the other three occur \(1298\) times.  
For the units digit the first seven terms of the cycle are  
\(7,4,\mathbf{1},8,\mathbf{5},\mathbf{2},\mathbf{9}\),  
so the digits that appear \(1299\) times are  

\[
1,2,4,5,7,8,9 .
\]

The same set of seven digits receives the extra occurrence for **every** decimal position, because the same cyclic order applies to each position when the modulus is increased by a factor of ten.

Thus, for each of the six positions the contribution of the odd digits is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{sum}_{\text{pos}} &=
1\cdot1299+3\cdot1298+5\cdot1299+7\cdot1299+9\cdot1299 \\[2pt]
&=1299+3894+6495+9093+11691 \\[2pt]
&=32\,472 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Since there are six decimal places, the total sum of all odd digits appearing in all the multiples of \(77\) below one million is  

\[
6 \times 32\,472 = 194\,832 .
\]

\[
\boxed{194832}
\]
